item.title: 'I want to develop myself more in the hills' –After another impressive punchy display at the Tour of Britain Women, is Lorena Wiebes evolving?
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: The seemingly invincible sprinting machine that is Lorena Wiebes rolled into Hay-on-Wye on Saturday afternoon, once again crossing the line first at the Tour of Britain Women for her third triumph in four days.Wiebes survived a host of GC attacks over the final categorised climbs of the 138km stage, a trek through mid-Wales which featured nearly 2,000 metres of elevation.Is she evolving into a sprinter-puncheur with an eye on the Ardennes, then?"I think not Liège, but Amstel Gold Race I would say yes, because also it's where I live at the moment. It's on my training roads, so it will become more and more a goal," Wiebes told after the finish."But I think year by year, it will become also harder to win Amstel because the whole peloton is improving and growing. But of course, I want to develop myself more in the hills and keep the sprint also, because if you see next year's Tour de France here in Britain, then it will be a tough one, so you will need it."Wiebes has grown stronger in the hills year on year, balancing that improvement with keeping her top-end sprint power."I think we are on the right path in that way. I think we really try to do it step-by-step, and that's also important to not lose the sprint too much," she said."So I think we're really in a good way. And I mean, also it's helpful that the team is helping with that, and like they trigger me also to become better."Wiebes will have another chance at victory on Sunday's finale in Leamington Spa, and on the largely flat stage, she's the overwhelming favourite. Stage win number four, along with Lippert finishing lower than third, would see her jump to a second overall on the final GC.The overall title is out of sight though, with Le Court-Pienaar holding a 35-second lead."Tomorrow it's another day of hard working, because I hope to pass Liane on GC to get into second place, of course."But it's already a successful Tour of Britain for us with three stage wins, and of course we aim for the GC podium now. The win is out of sight for GC, but we keep on fighting and try to go for another stage win tomorrow."With all this talk of winning, does she ever think about her future legacy and chasing records? Still only 27, Wiebes is now on 136, well short of Marianne Vos' 259. It looks like an unbreakable record, but given Wiebes' current win rate, who knows?"I think that will be really hard to chase Marianne, because she's still racing also!" she said. "No, I'm not really into that, but I mean, we want to win as much as possible, and hopefully I can keep it up for a few more years."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Deutschland Tour: Giulio Pellizzari wins queen stage as Isaac del Toro retakes control of race lead
item.content:encoded: Giulio Pellizzari (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) continued his strong August form by winning the queen stage of the Deutschland Tour, beating close friend off the bike, Isaac del Toro (UAE Team Emirates-XRG), to the line in Bad Dürkheim as the Mexican re-took the overall lead on stage 3.Del Toro attacked away from the peloton with 33km to go on the steepest climb of seven categorised ascents along the 170km route, the Rotsteig, where race leader Louis Barré (Visma-Lease a Bike) was unable to follow, but Pellizzari managed to bridge across. They rode the final 30km together after dropping lone early attacker Nelson Oliveira (Movistar) on the Annaberg, before arriving at the finish line where the Italian rode to the stage win and Del Toro back into the blue leader's jersey.Barré's team tried but failed to bring him back to the two leaders, and even several solo bursts couldn't see him limit the damage to less than the 49 seconds he shipped at the line. With one stage remaining on Sunday, Del Toro will start with a 52-second buffer over the Frenchman, which, if he successfully defends, will bring him his fourth stage race victory of the season."Today is a super day. Yesterday we were super happy with Magagnotti's win, so today we wanted to do it again, and it was the perfect day to do it," said Pellizzari after the stage,"We were in the perfect position when Isaac went. I just took my tempo and then in the end I came back. We had good collaboration – he was going for GC and I was going for the stage – we tried to do our best, and we are just super happy," he added, with both 22-year-old rising stars living in San Marino."We are super good friends, me and Isaac, of course, and during the race we have a good battle. I always say we are friends 1cm before the finish line; from there we are friends, so I'm super happy now he is leading in GC. Tomorrow is still one day; we will try with Alessio [Magagnotti], but today it's a perfect day for me, Isaac, and all San Marino."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: US Colleges Face a Shrinking Student Pipeline
item.content:encoded: US colleges are confronting a prolonged demographic squeeze as the number of high school graduates, after peaking in 2025, is projected to decline 13% through 2041, putting particular pressure on regional schools with limited endowments. Joining David Gura and Christina Ruffini on Bloomberg This Weekend is Carleton College Professor of Economics Nathan Grawe who explains that institutions are cutting programs, competing harder for students and emphasizing affordability and return on investment, while inflation-adjusted tuition at public four-year colleges has fallen 7% over the past decade. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Sanctions Target Iran’s Weakened Regional Network
item.content:encoded: The US is preparing a new campaign of economic pressure on Iran after diplomacy and months of fighting failed to produce a durable settlement, with President Donald Trump warning countries against maintaining trade ties with Tehran. Atlantic writer and Columbia University Institute of Global Politics Distinguished Fellow Kim Ghattas is on Bloomberg This Weekend and explains to hosts David Gura and Christina Ruffini that sanctions remain a blunt tool that will deepen hardship for ordinary Iranians, but Tehran’s weakened regional network and growing economic strain could make the latest pressure campaign different from those of the past 47 years. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Tour of Britain Women: Lorena Wiebes claims hard-fought hat trick of victories on stage 4
item.content:encoded: Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx-Protime) won her third Tour of Britain Women stage in four days, winning the sprint of a reduced group after a hilly stage 4 through Wales. Liane Lippert (Movistar) finished second, Kim Le Court-Pienaar (AG Insurance-Soudal) finished third and defended her GC lead.A breakaway of three was caught on the Hengoed climb, though not by the whole peloton as QOM jersey Lauren Dickson (FDJ United-Suez) had crashed, splitting the bunch.Things came back together after the climb, and Movistar did a lead-out into Clyro Hill, the last climb of the day where Lippert went all-in, quickly getting away with Le Court-Pienaar on her wheel.At the QOM point with 16.2km to go, they were four seconds ahead of Josie Nelson, Lorena Wiebes, Femke de Vries, and Shirin van Anrooij, and the four chasers closed the gap to the front duo together with Caroline Andersson (Liv AlUla Jayco).In a fast final, this front group of seven worked well together, but just after the 5km mark, a group of five came back from behind. There were several attacks in the final kilometres, but Wiebes closed them all down and then launched her sprint to win the stage.Going into the final stage, Le Court-Pienaar leads the GC by 24 seconds over Lippert and 29 seconds over Wiebes.The stage started in Llanidloes and covered 138.3km, winding through Powys before finishing in Hay-on-Wye, the “town of books” on the border to England.Fleur Moors (Lidl-Trek) went on a solo breakaway with over 121km to go, and the wearer of the white U23 jersey was 1:08 minutes ahead at the Elan Valley QOM. She increased her gap to 2:40 minutes with 90km to go while Juliana Londoño (Picnic PostNL) went on a solo chase.The Colombian never made it to Moors, though. She was passed by Alma Walther Møller Rasmussen (Hitec Products-Fluid Control) and caught by the peloton with 73km to go. Rasmussen continued to chase but only got within 1:35 minutes of Moors and was reeled in again 65km from the finish.Dilyxine Miermont (Picnic PostNL) attacked from the peloton on an unclassified climb out of Knighton with 58km to go. Alessia Vigilia (Uno-X Mobility) also went off the front with 50km to go, quickly bridging to Miermont, and together, they soon caught Moors to make it a front group of three, still over a minute ahead of the peloton where UAE Team L’IMAD, SD Worx-Protime, Canyon-SRAM, and Liv AlUla Jayco were now joining AG Insurance-Soudal at the front.At the bottom of the Hengoed climb, the gap was down to 57 seconds, and FDJ United-Suez were pulling hard in the peloton with Ally Wollaston and Kate Courtney leading out Dickson. Unfortunately for them, Dickson crashed after a touch of wheels with Courtney, splitting the peloton. Van Anrooij, Nelson, and Le Court-Pienaar bridged to the break on the climb, and another 14 riders also made it across just before the QOM.A group of 16 riders came back in the descent to make it a peloton of 36 riders at the front, and soon the attacks started. Katrine Aalerud (Uno-X Mobility) was first to try, then Mischa Bredewold (SD Worx-Protime) went with Cecilie Uttrup Ludwig (Canyon-SRAM). Alice Towers (Great Britain) and Ricarda Bauernfeind (Lidl-Trek) tried to jump across, but it was Le Court-Pienaar who closed the gap with Wiebes on her wheel.Van Anrooij was the next to attack but was closed down by Karlijn Swinkels (UAE Team L’IMAD) after a short chase, an attack by Bredewold and a Movistar rider was neutralised by a Le Court-Pienaar, and the following move by De Vries was shut down by Marit Raaijmakers (Human Powered Health).After Vigilia’s attack was reeled in by Uttrup Ludwig and Towers, Movistar took over at the front of the group to lead out Lippert into the 2.2km climb up Clyro Hill with three riders. Lippert went hard on the steep ramp at the start of the climb and got a gap with Le Court-Pienaar on her wheel, taking everybody else by surprise.On the flatter section in the middle of the climb, Bredewold had taken up the chase in the peloton, and as the gradient kicked up again, Nelson, De Vries, Wiebes, Van Anrooij, and Andersson attacked from the bunch.Five seconds behind at the top, the five chasers closed the gap 14km from the finish while Dickson crashed a second time. Erica Magnaldi (UAE Team L’IMAD) and Swinkels, only seven seconds behind at the QOM, were left chasing in vain, eventually sitting up to join forces with Pfeiffer Georgi (Picnic PostNL), Kate Courtney (FDJ United-Suez), and Marte Berg Edseth (Uno-X Mobility).The five chasers closed the gap with 4.6km to go, and after Wiebes shut down an attack by Courtney, Magnaldi began to set the pace with Wiebes on her wheel until Swinkels tried to attack from the very back of the group, just over 2km from the line.Again, Wiebes had no trouble in neutralising the attack, and when De Vries and Edseth tried to get away, Wiebes shut their move down too. Andersson and Magnaldi also tried to attack but didn’t even keep going past Wiebes, who was attentive to everything, leading the group onto the finishing straight while two groups came back in touch on the final kilometre.Van Anrooij tried one last move at the 500m mark but had Swinkels in her wheel, who then opened the sprint with 250m to go. Wiebes, Le Court-Pienaar, and Lippert reacted immediately, and Wiebes pulled ahead in the last 100 metres to win the stage by almost two bike lengths to Lippert, who came around Le Court-Pienaar to take second place.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Small Dogs, Big Demand as Dachshund Popularity Takes Off
item.content:encoded: Dachshunds are enjoying a global popularity boom, climbing to No. 5 in the American Kennel Club’s 2025 rankings as owners embrace their small size and outsized personalities. The surge is supporting everything from breed meetups to dachshund cafes, even as owners contend with health concerns including intervertebral disc disease, which may affect roughly one in four dachshunds. Joining Bloomberg This Weekend to discuss all things Dachshund is Bloomberg News Bangkok Bureau Chief Randy Thanthong-Knight. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Russia Considers Grain Purchases to Offset Export Disruptions
item.author: Bloomberg News
item.content:encoded: Russia’s government is planning a series of measures to support grain producers, include crop procurement, preferential loan extensions and sales subsidies, Interfax reported, citing Agriculture Minister Oksana Lut.

item.title: Study Shows AI Hitting Paychecks, Not Payrolls
item.content:encoded: Apollo Chief Economist Torsten Slok says early labor-market data suggest AI’s first impact is appearing more in wages than employment. In a study of hundreds of occupations, Slok found that jobs with higher exposure to AI have seen weaker wage growth, while the employment effect remains relatively small. But the picture is still coming into focus: Slok says AI is also helping fuel record business formation, which could create new jobs and make the economy more dynamic. Former IBM HR chief Diane Gherson says companies are already deciding which work can be automated, which employees can be retrained and whether AI savings come through layoffs, slower hiring or reskilling. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Renewi Tour: Jasper Philipsen awarded photo-finish sprint to claim stage 4 victory, retakes leader's jersey
item.content:encoded: Another photo-finish at the 2026 Renewi Tour saw Jasper Philipsen (Alpecin-Premier Tech) emerge victorious on stage 4, narrowly pipping Olav Kooij (Decathlon CMA CGM) to the line in Bilzen-Hoeselt after a tight sprint.Kooij came off the wheel of Biniam Girmay (NSN) in the final 200 metres with his eyes on the line and most of his rivals fading, but Philipsen was still lurking in his slipstream and struck in the final 75 metres to beat him with a good bike throw by a tyre's width.There was another crash at the Belgian WorldTour race, with Søren Wærenskjold (Uno-X Mobility) coming down in the final 500 metres, but most of the big names managed to avoid it.Alessandro Borgo (Bahrain-Victorious) came through late to finish third on stage, beating Dylan Groenewegen (Unibet Rose Rockets), who opened up the final sprint following a strong lead-out, with Luca Mozzato (Tudor) rounding out the top five.Philipsen moved back into the overall lead of the race ahead of stage 3 winner Jenno Berckmoes (Lotto Intermarché), who failed to get up there in the sprint and couldn't get away from his rivals despite strong work from Arnaud De Lie leading into the final rep of the many punchy climbs along the 187km route.Philipsen will take a four-second lead over his compatriot into the final day in and around Leuven, the site of the 2021 World Championships."It was a hard day, didn't have the freshest legs in the end, but I didn't think anybody had. So in the end I was happy I could launch my sprint just in time to overtake Olav," said Philipsen after his eighth win in 2026 so far."It was a really close sprint and a strong sprint from him, so I'm happy I could take victory. Of course it was a very tough day with the weather conditions, and it wasn't easy either with the hills on the course. A tough day and tomorrow also will be another tough day."Sprinters battle it out after tough fourth stageWhile the fourth stage of the Renewi Tour was always expected to be one for the sprinters, a tough course through Belgian Limburg lined with 14 short and sharp hills meant it was never going to be an easy day, with constantly changing weather conditions on Saturday adding another variable to the difficulty. Racing split with 130km to go, when a six-man breakaway went up the road: Axel Huens, Johan Jacobs (Groupama-FDJ United), Kamil Małecki (Pinarello Q36.5), Lionel Taminiaux (Lotto Intermarché), Aivaras Mikutis (Tudor), Toms Skujiņš (Lidl-Trek).While they went a minute up the road, 16 riders did briefly break away from the peloton to form a second group, but they were quickly caught, and the race settled into a regular sprint stage chasing pattern, with the likes of Alpecin-Premier Tech, Soudal-QuickStep and Netcompany Ineos doing the lion's share of the work. The break did survive out in front until the Green KM, where Taminiaux and Mikutis shared the three sprint wins. From here, though, the Belgian dropped back while the Lithuanian champion kicked on to be the last man standing up the road, alongside Małecki, before they were fulled caught back with 21km to go. Action in the peloton didn't settle, even with a sprint now looking certain, as Lidl-Trek – who are without sprinter Jonathan Milan after he crashed on stage 2 and abandoned one day later – sent Søren Kragh Andersen up the road with 17km to go. His attack was working well until he reached the final lap up the Letenberg climb, where Arnaud De Lie accelerated in support of Berckmoes and all but fully ended the Dane's move. However, as the pace lulled due to no one wanting to push on, he was just able to re-establish a lead. Kragh Andersen would survive all the way into the final kilometre, where he was caught by Unibet Rose Rockets and Soudal-QuickStep working on the front for a sprint. As the finale played out, though, both those teams would miss out as Groenewegen and Tim Merlier failed to match the much faster Philipsen and Kooij.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Vuelta a España stage 1 LIVE: Kluckers betters Brennan's benchmark in opening ITT, but Pogačar and Van Aert still to come
item.content:encoded: For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. You'll get comprehensive race coverage of La Vuelta a España, subscriber-exclusive analysis from our expert columnists, in-depth features and industry-leading tech insight. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go! August 22, 2026 – 9:57 AMHola and welcome to stage one of the 2026 Vuelta a España!August 22, 2026 – 10:04 AMIt’s time at last for the Vuelta a España, the final Grand Tour of the season! After all the thrills of the Tour de France in July and Tour de France Femmes in August, the attention of the cycling world now turns to Spain.Much like in France, it’s the same man who is hogging all of the attention - Tadej Pogačar The Slovenian is going into this race as even more of a favourite than he was for the Tour, and the world is braced for another special performance from him. Pogačar himself, though, is stressing the need to approach intelligently, and not take things for granted.August 22, 2026 – 10:08 AMPogačar and the other GC contenders’ quest for the red jersey begins with a short, flat, but technical time trial in Monaco. It’s not long enough to cause especially big gaps between the GC contenders, but there’s been much talk about the tricky corners - anyone wanting a high GC finish will have to be careful not to make a mistake. August 22, 2026 – 10:14 AMIn terms of the stage win today, there’s very healthy competition among some quality time trialists all vying for the honor of wearing the red jersey. Pogačar is inevitably a contender, but will be up against specialists like Wout van Aert and Josh Tarling. Here’s the full running order of the day.August 22, 2026 – 10:18 AMThe first rider is Diego Uriarte, and he rolls down the start ramp to get this year's Vuelta a España underway!August 22, 2026 – 10:26 AMThere are no real curve balls in the running order, with most of the top riders not setting off until later in the day. But there is one man already out that's worth keeping an eye on - Markel Beloki. As the son of Joseba, he has the genes, and based on some of his performances since turning pro, he has the talent too. August 22, 2026 – 10:32 AMKaden Groves is the latest to start. The Australian is on a mission to win what would be a third points classification at this race. But he's unlikely to score any points today. The time trial might be short, but not quite short enough for a sprinter like himself.August 22, 2026 – 10:37 AMAfter taking off first, Diego Uriarte (pictured) has the fastest time at the finish, and none of the five riders who have joined him at the clubhouse so far have manage to better him. But his time is under threat by Andreas Leknessund, who is quicker than him at the intermediate check.August 22, 2026 – 10:41 AMUriarte’s time has indeed been beaten, by three riders in quick succession - Beloki, Porter, then Leknessund, who has gone quicker by a whole nine seconds. He might have faced some stiff competition from Bruno Armirail, one of the few time trial specialists who have set off early, but the Frenchman’s hopes have been dashed by a mechanical. August 22, 2026 – 10:47 AMA Norwegian has been usurped by a Dane! Lidl's Norsgaard pips Leknessund's time by a mere second, after Kaden Groves had himself fallen just one second short. Meanwhile at the start, the first major GC contender has just began - Richard Carapaz. After his star attacking turn at the Tour de France, he's stated his intent to commit fully to GC at this race, so will go hard to concede as little time as possible.August 22, 2026 – 10:52 AMAnother new leader is in the clubhouse, and this time by a big margin, as 23-year-old Jordan Labrosse (pictured) bests Norsgaard by a whole 16 seconds. That's a mighty impressive ride, but even he was challenged moments later as sprinter Aulaur came within a second of beating him at the finish. August 22, 2026 – 11:01 AMRichard Carapaz has finished his ride, and it looks pretty solid. He's third fastest, with a time ten seconds slower than Labrosse. We'll have a much better idea of how good it is later on, once the other non-time trial specialist GC riders start their rides.A couple of other such rider have just rolled off the start ramp - Matthew Riccitello, and former winner Sepp Kuss. Unlike Carapaz, they are only outside contenders, and may not go hard today if they're not targetting it. August 22, 2026 – 11:08 AMLabrosse’s time is safe for now, with nobody threatening it at the intermediate time check.While there’s a slight lull in what has been a hectic start, be sure to catch up on what’s happened at both the Renewi Tour and Tour of Britain Women, both of which have finished. August 22, 2026 – 11:16 AMSepp Kuss has just finished, 22 seconds with the 13th fastest ride. That didn't appear to be a ride from someone going as hard as possible to limit his losses, but nor did he sit up and take it easy.The 2023 champion has said that is prioritising chasing stage wins over the GC, but that ride suggests he isn't totally sacrificing the former just yet. August 22, 2026 – 11:24 AMFor the first time in his career, Matthew Brennan is riding at a Grand Tour! He's just started his ride, bringing to a beginning a Vuelta debut which has attracted much hype. This probably won't be a day for him, but he has his eyes on the sprints, which he is a genuine contender for a win based on his brilliant form this season. August 22, 2026 – 11:32 AMA couple more significant GC times to report. Both Mattias Skjelmose (6th at the Tour de France this year) and Tobias Halland Johannessen (6th at the Tour de France last year) have finished 5 seconds slower than Laborsse, and are placed 4th and 3rd respectively on the virtual classification. Skjelmose might have wanted to go quicker than that, given how the time trial is usually one of his big weapons. August 22, 2026 – 11:34 AMA turn up for the books here - Sander De Pestel has just posted the best time, five seconds faster than his Decathlon teammate Labrosse. What did the Decathlon riders eat today for lunch? Whatever it is it's working, as they're on fire.De Pestel might not be in the hot seat for long though, as Brennan is flying and has the fastest time at the intermediate check. Watch this space...August 22, 2026 – 11:37 AMThe Brit has indeed gone faster, beating De Pestel by two seconds! That's one hell of a ride from Brennan, especially considering it's the sprint we're anticipating him making an impact at this Vuelta, rather than the time trial. He's a huge talent whose versatility could become one of the stories of this race. And he was also one of the young riders we picked to look out for ahead of the race. Have a read to see who else we're backing, in a race where young talent often comes to the fore.August 22, 2026 – 11:44 AMOscar Onley is off an underway! Following an injury-disrupted start to the season, this will be his first Grand Tour since placing fourth at the Tour de France last year. Given the form he showed at the Vuelta a Burgos, he's one of the top candidates for a podium finish overall, so will race hard today.August 22, 2026 – 11:49 AMFor unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. You'll get comprehensive race coverage of La Vuelta a España, subscriber-exclusive analysis from our expert columnists, in-depth features and industry-leading tech insight. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!August 22, 2026 – 11:53 AMAnother top name for the podium is on the road now, and, all things considered, is going OK. Felix Gall is 16th fastest at the time check, only 3 seconds slower than Carapaz and five seconds slower than Skjelmose. For a man whose Achilles' heel is the time trial, he will take this. August 22, 2026 – 11:59 AMOnley and Gall (pictured) have both now finished, and they’ve both set similar times - both losing quite a bit of time. Onley was well down in with the 40th fastest time, losing 34 seconds to Brennan, while Gall (though normally the inferior time trialist) limited his losses to 30 seconds with the 33rd fastest time. Much quicker is young Pablo Torres, who has gone 6th quickest so far at his first ever stage at a Grand Tour. August 22, 2026 – 12:09 PMBrennan has been ousted from the hot seat! Kluckers had gone 2 seconds quicker at the time check, and extended that to 4 seconds by the finish. He might have finished 6th at the Tour of Poland time trial recently, but that's still a surprising ride from the Luxembourger

item.title: American Whiskey Pays Price for Canada Trade Rift
item.content:encoded: US spirits exports to Canada fell 70% from March through December 2025 after most provinces removed American alcohol from their shelves, while exports elsewhere rose 2.5%. American Whiskey Association President & CEO Michael Bilello is on Bloomberg This Weekend and says restoring market access is only the first challenge, American whiskey producers also need to rebuild demand among Canadian consumers after more than a year of trade tensions. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: MI6 Veteran Warns Against Politicizing Intelligence
item.content:encoded: Former Head of MI6 Sir Richard Dearlove joins Christina Ruffini on Bloomberg This Weekend to discuss the current state of the international intelligence community. Dearlove says that UK-US intelligence cooperation remains close but expressed concern about politicization and personnel changes inside the CIA, an issue that has also drawn scrutiny amid broader changes across the US intelligence community. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Ajayi and Mendy give Hull dream start against misfiring Manchester United
item.author: Will Unwin at the MKM Stadium
item.content:encoded: Ever since Sir Alex Ferguson’s retirement 13 years ago, Manchester United have been stuck in football’s equivalent of purgatory and a chastening experience in Hull suggests they could be there a while longer. Michael Carrick’s permanent appointment was supposed to hail a new era at Old Trafford but very little has changed based on this defeat.United were sluggish from start to finish and rightly punished for failing to defend set pieces with any degree of competence. Centre-backs Semi Ajayi and Nobel Mendy earned Hull the prized scalp upon their return to the Premier League while United are left to ponder if the squad requires more invasive surgery before the transfer window closes.Continue reading...

item.title: Cycling's next generation heads to Spain –Young riders to watch at the Vuelta a España
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: The future is now, and it's coming to the Vuelta a España as a host of the sport's top young riders head to Spain for the final Grand Tour of the season.This year's trek around Spain – starting from Monaco and ending in Granada – is, on paper, more challenging than both the Giro d'Italia and the Tour de France. It features a mammoth 58,156 metres of elevation, well above its sister Grand Tours.That fact, plus the presence of the world's most dominant rider, Tadej Pogačar, hasn't put off some of the youngest riders in the WorldTour peloton from heading to Spain. Among the host of youngsters at the Vuelta are 15 riders aged 21 or under, including four 20-year-olds.These riders, ranging from climbers and future GC hopefuls to Classics-style fast finishers and those just hoping to learn at their first Grand Tour proving ground, will face an arduous task ahead, battling the late-summer Spanish heat and seven summit finishes.We've decided to omit a handful of young riders from our list even if they meet the criteria for the white best young rider's jersey. For example, the likes of Oscar Onley, Matthew Riccitello, and Cian Uijtdebroeks are proven GC contenders with top Grand Tour results to their name. In the high mountains and summit finishesBelgian racer Jarno Widar has been populating lists of up-and-coming GC starlets for some time now. He lit up the junior ranks with wins at races including the Tour of Flanders, National Championships, Classique des Alpes, Philippe Gilbert Juniors, and Kuurne-Brussel-Kuurne. Then, in 2024, he won the Alpes Isère Tour, Giro d'Italia Next Gen, and Giro della Valle d'Aosta. Last season, he won the Ronde de l'Isard and Valle d'Aosta before finishing second behind Paul Seixas at the Tour de l'Avenir.Still just 20, he's already racked up a series of promising results in his first year as a pro with Lotto, despite a knee injury early in the season. Standouts include fourth places on Malhão at the Volta ao Algarve, in Villars-sur-Olon at the Tour de Suisse, and on the Pineda de la Sierra at the recent Vuelta a Burgos."I know the Vuelta route practically by heart. Burgos might give me some indication of what to expect. And do you know what I've got to do after Burgos? The most tedious training sessions you can imagine – putting on as many layers of clothing as possible and then training on the rollers in the heat. I'm not looking forward to the heat, but I'm preparing for it," he told two weeks ago.In Burgos, Widar fell ill with an infection, but will hopefully be back to full health for the Vuelta, where there's no pressure on a big GC ride, his team has said. He hasn't raced more than eight consecutive days in his career to date, so his debut Grand Tour at the Vuelta a España will be a big next step, but he'll certainly be one to watch on select mountain days. Flat finishes, breakaway days, possibly the green jersey fightBy now, Matthew Brennan is a known quantity, which is incredible to say of a 21-year-old. The Briton only turned pro last year and finished his neo-pro season ranked seventh in wins in world cycling.His victories included the cobbles (GP de Denain), hilly WorldTour days (four stages across the Volta a Catalunya, Tour de Romandie, and Tour de Pologne), and flat sprints (three stages at the Deutschland Tour and Tour of Britain).He's scored seven more this season, with Kuurne-Brussel-Kuurne the standout result, and he's in fine form heading to the Vuelta, too. He won two stages at the Vuelta a Burgos, the first of which came in a one-two with Visma teammate Ben Tulett, another youngster racing here.Those victories came on hillier days rather than pan-flat sprints, suggesting that he and Wout van Aert should combine as a fearsome duo in the battle for the green jersey against Mads Pedersen. Like Widar, Brennan will be training hard to adapt to the sweltering temperatures in Spain."I was slowly roasting from the inside out," Brennan said after his second win in Burgos. "I’m glad I could finish it off in the end because it was a tough day in the heat. It felt like we were riding through a desert all day."Stage hunter, domestique Breakaways on hilly and mountain stagesThis rapid rise comes after the 22-year-old started slowly as a junior in Australia before a message from Simon Clarke kick-started his European racing career, he wrote in his column for earlier this season.He joined Trinity as an under-23, racing to top-10 finishes at the Ronde de l'Isard and Giro Next Gen, before switching to the Red Bull Rookies setup last year. The resulting spell in pink and overall second place at the Giro Next Gen saw him sign his first WorldTour contract.This week, Tuckwell wrote about his Vuelta preparation for . A family illness made his pre-race altitude training camp more challenging, while he rode strongly at the Vuelta a Burgos, equalling his best-ever 20-minute power output before falling ill ahead of the final stage.Like several others on this list, Tuckwell has never tackled such a long race before – "I'm also getting slightly nervous about what lies ahead," he wrote – but he's also excited about the challenge and excited to pen more dispatches from Spain.GC leader, stage hunter In the hills, mountains, and possibly breakawaysGerman rider Marco Brenner has not yet lived up to the massive hype that surrounded him as he swept almost all before him as a junior. This season, his third at Tudor, has been his best yet since turning pro at 18 back in 2021, though.The former German road champion started his season in good form with fourth place at the Tour Down Under and fourth at the Tour des Alpes-Maritimes before racing to a top-10 finish at the Boucles de la Mayenne. He heads to the Vuelta with the best result of his career to date in the bag, too, having triumphed at the recent Tour de Pologne after a week of consistent riding.He'll take confidence from that and from a newly signed contract extension to 2030, and he'll have freedom to race for his own results in Spain. Tudor have no top GC rider or sprinter to protect, so he and Will Barta will be "targeting the decisive climbing stages, both eager to break new ground as they take on the challenge of Grand Tour leadership", the team says.The Vuelta will be his second outing at the race, having made his Grand Tour debut here four years ago. Back then, his best result was fifth place from the break on the summit finish of Estepona behind Richard Carapaz. Watch out for him in the hills and mountains again this time around. Working in Tadej Pogačar's mountain trainSpanish talent Pablo Torres, 20, will be keenly watched by home fans, even if he's set to spend the race working for Tadej Pogačar, rather than riding for his own chances.Torres is from a cycling family, with his brother and sister, both 18, also riding for UAE among the development setup.The trio hail from Madrid, and Torres will one day hope to emulate several other riders from the region, including past Grand Tour stars Alberto Contador and Carlos Sastre. This Vuelta marks his Grand Tour debut, though, so it may be a while before he can reach a similar level.Torres won plenty in the junior ranks, while a glittering 2024 saw him take second places at the Giro Next Gen and Tour de l'Avenir, winning the Colle delle Finestre mountain stage at the latter by almost four minutes.Last season, his first in the pro ranks, was a learning year, while this year he has a narrow bronze in the Spanish TT Championships and 11th at the Vuelta a Burgos to his name. Torres should slot in among Pavel Sivakov, João Almeida, and Jay Vine to do the work for Pogačar in the mountains, so we should see him pushing some big watts in the Sierra Nevada in the coming weeks.Stage hunter, puncheur Hilly stages rather than high mountainsPaul Seixas may have been the talk of the cycling world this season, the 19-year-old phenom having raced to fourth at the Tour de France last month, but he's not the only young talent on the French Decathlon CMA CGM team. Step forward 21-year-old Léo Bisiaux, a former fourth-place finisher at the Tour de l'Avenir now in his second season as a pro.Bisiaux has already made his Grand Tour debut, racing last year's Vuelta in support of Felix Gall, and he headed into the race with third place and a stage win at the Vuelta a Burgos.This year he's been stronger still, scoring podiums at the Tour du Jura and Mercan'Tour Classic Alpes-Maritimes, 10th at the Donostia San Sebastián Klasikoa, and 12th at Liège-Bastogne-Liège. He took seventh at the Vuelta a Burgos this year, also taking home the best young rider jersey in the process as he supported Gall to overall victory.Bisiaux will again be at the service of the Austrian climber and US racer Matthew Riccitello in the high mountains but should get his own chances here and there, too.Domestique, puncheur, time triallist Monaco TT, hilly stages, working for team leadersIván Romeo has been around a while, having turned pro with Movistar back in 2023, but the Spaniard's story has been one of gradual progress rather than a single big breakthrough, and this year he's stepped up another level again.The man from Valladolid is one for the hills rather than high mountains. He's a strong time triallist, too, having been under-23 world champion in the discipline and finished seventh in the Caen TT at last year's Tour de France.He raced the past year as Spanish road champion, while this year's top results have included overall victory at the Vuelta a Andalucía – ahead of Tom Pidcock – plus a stage win and fifth overall at O Gran Camiño. A successful lead-in to the Vuelta saw him race to third overall at the recent Tour de Pologne.This debut at his home Grand Tour will see him working for Movistar leaders Cian Uijtdebroeks and Enric Mas, though he should get opportunities to send it in the hills – and watch out for him in the opening time trial in Monaco. Mountain stages, breakawaysWhile Brennan will be active in the sprints for Visma-Lease a Bike, the Dutch squad have another young rider for the hills and mountains. Norwegian racer Jørgen Nordhagen is their man, with no Jonas Vingegaard or Matteo Jorgenson in the line-up. Instead, he'll look to former race winner Sepp Kuss for guidance.The 21-year-old was a top prospect in the junior ranks, winning the Course de la Paix and Eroica Juniores before joining the Visma development setup, winning the Giro Friulio Venezia Giulia before taking fourth at the Giro Next Gen and third at the Tour de l'Avenir.His progression has continued this season, with a second place at O Gran Camiño and a fourth at the Tour de Romandie among his highlight results. A seventh place at Lagunas de Neila at the recent Vuelta a Burgos shows he has his climbing legs for his Grand Tour debut.Stage hunter, puncheur Hilly stagesNys has attributed his illness to eating a contaminated steak tartare during a team training camp in Mallorca. He's undergone a 12-day course of antibiotics to be fit for the Vuelta, and will now return to racing as part of Lidl-Trek's selection.The German team will be competing on several fronts in Spain, with Mattias Skjelmose aiming for a top GC result to go with his sixth place at the Tour de France, and fellow Dane Mads Pedersen targeting the sprints and another points jersey, having won two here before.Nys, who in 2024 won stages at the Tour de Romandie, Tour de Suisse, and Tour de Pologne, will surely be looking to add to his palmarès in Spain. This will be his second Grand Tour after last year's Tour de France, and there are a host of stages that fit his profile as a punchy, explosive rider. He's lacking in race fitness, however, with only seven race days to his name this season – all back in June."It is a year to forget quickly, but I hope to be able to turn things around in the Vuelta," he told Belgian radio station JOE. "It didn't look good for a long time. My coach and I had already buried the hatchet when it suddenly turned around. I feel ready for it. We are going from a lot of doubt to a feeling that something is possible after all." Working for team leader Richard CarapazBasque racer Markel Beloki heads to his second career Vuelta a España after making his Grand Tour debut at last year's race. The 21-year-old has impressed in his second year among the WorldTour peloton, with a win at the Tour de l'Ain his highlight performance.His surname shows his pedigree – he's the son of Joseba, a four-time Grand Tour podium finisher and runner-up at the 2002 Tour de France. If he can come close to emulating his father, then he'll have a very successful career; that much is certain.This Vuelta, he'll be working for EF Education-EasyPost leader and GC hopeful Richard Carapaz, rather than going for his own chances. He's in strong form, too, having taken eighth place at the recent Vuelta a Burgos. "During the season I had my own opportunities in different kinds of races, but now I'll try to help the team as much as I can. That's the main objective for the next three weeks," Beloki said recently."I am climbing really well, so I can be close to him when he needs it on the climbs, or helping make a selection of riders."Alpecin-Premier Tech head to the Vuelta without their two big stars, Mathieu van der Poel and Jasper Philipsen. Instead, the departing Kaden Groves leads the way, having won seven stages and two points jerseys in Spain. 20-year-old will be looking to learn from the Australian during his first Grand Tour. The Belgian is a fast finisher and has four top-10 finishes to his name in this, his neo-pro season.The Belgian squad also features another promising youngster in 23-year-old . Another Belgian, he's starting his second Grand Tour of the year after racing the first 13 days of the Tour de France earlier this summer. Standout results to date include 13th at the Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, 18th at Liège-Bastogne-Liège, and fifth place on the hilly day to Foix at the Tour. He'll have freedom to be active in the hills and mountains.Slovenia's talent machine keeps on churning, with 20-year-old the latest promising youngster to hit the pro ranks. The Bahrain Victorious rider won the Giro d'Italia Next Gen last year, and he's taken third place at the Tour of Slovenia and sixth at the Tour of the Alps this season.In addition to Brennan, another British rider to watch will be Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe's , like Tuckwell another neo-pro at the German team. The 23-year-old is a time trial specialist and will be one to watch on the opening day in Monaco. Last year he was under-23 national champion and won a very short closing time trial at the Sibiu Tour, and he heads to the Vuelta with a top-three in the Tour de Pologne's closing TT in his pocket.Widar, Nys, Sentjens, and Debruyne are joined on our list by another Belgian in the form of Lotto-Intermarché's 21-year-old, . A fast finisher, he's racing his second year in the pros and scored a host of good results in the spring. He was second at the GP La Marseillaise on his first day of the season and also has top-10 finishes at Nokere Koerse, the Bredene Koksijde Classic, and Scheldeprijs to his name.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'You will have to use the brakes' – Tadej Pogačar and rest of Vuelta a España contenders brace themselves for very technical opening time trial in Monaco
item.content:encoded: With over 58,000 metres of vertical climbing, the 2026 Vuelta a España has been described by its race director Javier Guillén as the hardest he's ever seen. But this evening's very short opening time trial in the streets of Monaco could be one of the most technical in the race's history, too.Featuring multiple corners over just 9.4 kilometres and with 170 metres of climbing out of the 2026 Vuelta's total of over 58,000, as leading favourite Tadej Pogačar put it in his pre-race press conference, "it's not going to be a 60kmh flat-out time trial. You will have to use the brakes."Due to start his time trial at 19:19 local time on what looks set to be a warm, dry evening in Monaco, Pogačar promised to give it everything on the course, but warned that the chances that he could be wearing la roja just a few streets away from his current home are not overly high.But despite knowing the roads very well, the UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider said he would do a good recon of the course to minimise any potential risks."You just need to go a bit slower in the corners. That’s it," Pogačar said on Thursday when asked about comments by Wout van Aert – a top favourite for Saturday, who has even gone so far as to recreate his own simulation of the time trial route to practice on it, according to - that "the organisers have pushed the limits with this route.""I know the roads really, really well. I go with the motorbike, I go with the car, I go with the bike, I walk them. It’s not ideal, but it's not going to be a 60 kilometres per hour flat-out time trial," said Pogačar."You will have to use the brakes and use a bit of a different pacing strategy than what we are used to."Pogačar argued that on the recon, once the route had been barriered off, it would be possible to see the riskier corners and work out how to tackle them best. He also pointed to similarities between the course and the race-opening TT in Copenhagen in the 2022 Tour – although thankfully the weather in Monaco promises to be better than in Denmark, where rain made it much tougher for the late starters and top contenders."It's pretty technical; it reminds me a little bit of the Copenhagen time trial in the [2022] Tour de France; we also went through one garden, a sidewalk or something."In the end, every rider needs to manage their own effort. It can be as technical as it can be, but it's up to each rider about how fast they go."It has to be said that Pogačar does not have great memories of opening time trials in the Vuelta. In 2019's opening team time trial on the course in Torrevieja near Alicante,in a somewhat surreal turn of events, a child's bathing pool in a nearby garden burst during the race and water spilt downhill and out onto the course. Several teams, including UAE and Jumbo-Visma, crashed and fell as a result.Given his success rate in the sport overall, though, Pogačar can never be ruled out of any event he starts in, and he promised to make an all-out effort to take the only Grand Tour leader's jersey still missing from his palmares on day 1. “I’m going to give everything. The first stage will not be easy for me. I will do my best, but the competition for the first day will be very high," he said."There are guys who will be very fast and who are very technical, who will be very fast on this course. I will try; I just want to start the race, go there and see how it is.”For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!

item.title: Julian Alaphilippe had more than panache – he was a conjuror who was greater than the sum of his watts
item.content:encoded: Four weeks ago, Julian Alaphilippe flopped to the tarmac just by my feet at the top of Alpe d’Huez. The Frenchman wasn’t high up my list of people to speak to at the finish line of the penultimate stage of the Tour de France, but it soon became clear he couldn’t be ignored.With his arms stretched out behind him, and the media swarming the new French hope Paul Seixas in front of him, Alaphilippe sat staring into the middle distance.It was a loaded moment, and one that makes even more sense in the light of the news of his sudden retirement from the sport.When Alaphilippe, still sitting on the tarmac, finally spoke to the media, he sounded like a man not long for this sport. "I’m not thinking about tomorrow. I’m thinking about nothing at all. All I really want is to hold my son in my arms," he said quietly.He suggested, repeatedly and with varying levels of ambiguity, that this would be his final Tour de France. And he went on to make a comment that was telling at the time and even more so in hindsight."No, no. There is no enjoyment there anymore," he said of his experience at this year’s Tour. "It’s OK, it’s over. It’s time to stop when there is no more enjoyment."That last line could, of course, be taken out of context. In actual fact, Alaphilippe was referring to the interview, standing up as he very subtly declared the exchange over. But he knew what he was doing; there was a mischievous twinkle in his eye as he delivered the double entendre.My gut instinct at that moment was that Alaphilippe was as good as done with cycling. But then again, I also suspected that the emotion of the moment was taking over and, in the cold light of day, when this dispiriting Tour de France was in the rearview mirror, he may well take stock and feel differently about 2027.It wasn’t to be. Julian Alaphilippe is done. Time waits for no man, and one of the great careers of the 21st century is boxed up and packaged away.In the 24 hours that separated the reports of Alaphilippe’s retirement and his announcement, social media had been flooded with tributes, not just from fans but from race organisers, broadcasters, and fellow riders. The news was not even confirmed at that point, but seemingly no one could hold back in pouring out their respects and admiration for a rider who captured the imagination like few others.If there was such an overwhelming response to Alaphilippe’s exit, then it’s probably because of the way he made you feel.Yes, there was panache, of course there was – buckets of the stuff. But it was something more than that.Alaphilippe was pure electricity. And like lightning in a charged sky, he connected in bright, powerful flashes. In fact, I struggle to think of another rider who has connected with fans on quite the same visceral level. He didn’t so much put you on the edge of your seat as reach through the television and pull you into the race.There are many entries on the Alaphilippe highlights reel, from the way he lit up the 2019 Tour de France with that 14-day stint in yellow, all the way down to the less favourable moments such as the Liège-Bastogne-Liège he threw away in 2020.But for me, his second World Championship title in Leuven in 2021 was the pinnacle – his magnum opus, and the embodiment of Julian Alaphilippe.He came into that title defence without great form or hope – and he later revealed that on some level he’d be happy to have the weight of the rainbow jersey off his shoulders. But from somewhere he summoned one of the greatest performances the Worlds has seen.He threw caution to the wind, he attacked again and again, and he held off the chasers on a nail-biting final lap, all while pulling faces to the TV cameras and whipping up the crowds.It was heavy metal cycling from a master showman. But this was also a conjuror at work, producing something – through instinct, inspiration, and sheer heart – that was greater than the sum of its watts. It was a sort of magic.Sitting in his post-race press conference in Leuven, Alaphilippe made a striking comment that has always stuck with me."Since 2014, I’m still the same rider, and I don’t want to change anything," he said. "I took a lot of pleasure in riding like this and for me it’s really important to keep this pleasure, because cycling is a hard sport, and I don’t want to become a robot."Alaphilippe turned professional in 2014 in the middle of the Team Sky era, when the British team rode with such control and precision that their riders were widely referred to as 'Skybots'. He retires in an era where, even if panache is in safe hands with the likes of Pogačar and Van der Poel, the life of a pro cyclist is marinated in data and increasingly mapped out by artificial intelligence.In between, Alaphilippe carved out a space where emotional energy was the guiding force, where he could fail spectacularly but win even more so, and where you never quite knew what was going to happen next.In the end, cycling caught up with Alaphilippe, and left him behind. Not that he didn’t rage against the dying of the light. His Giro d’Italia stage win in 2024 – won via a 120-kilometre attack – was one of his most audacious exploits, and the 2025 Grand Prix de Québec was taken out with an opportunistic heist. It would prove to be his final victory.There were no such flickers of the old Alaphilippe in 2026, and the Tour de France turned out to be a struggle and little more. At Alpe d’Huez he crossed the line arm in arm with Warren Barguil, a fellow declining Frenchman who days earlier had made headlines with his comments on cycling’s new generation. "Before, if you did 6 watts per kilo, you were good," Barguil said. "Now, you’re a teammate."Alaphilippe agreed. "Yes, yes. You feel that. And I think you see it too. The speeds are crazy," he said.Alaphilippe had one year left on his contract, but, as ever, his heart told him something different to the numbers. Perhaps he could have squeezed another season, but he’d have been going through the motions, and that, ultimately, made no sense to him.And so Alaphilippe acted on instinct and improvised his own retirement – on-brand to the very last.He leaves a legacy, with 45 professional victories, six Tour de France stages, and two world titles. But above all, he’ll be remembered for the way he made you feel.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'A top 10 on GC isn't as important as a stage win' – 2023 Vuelta a España champion Sepp Kuss to make definitive decision on overall bid at end of first week
item.content:encoded: In some ways, we've been here before. When Sepp Kuss rolls down the start line of the Monaco time trial on Saturday in the Vuelta a España, just like in 2023, the Visma-Lease a Bike racer will be tackling his third Grand Tour of the season.The crunch question being: will Kuss be aiming to do what he did in 2023 and end up going for the overall win in the Vuelta, too?After two 13th-place finishes at the Giro d'Italia and Tour de France this season, as well as a stage win in the Giro, when he talks about the Vuelta, the American invariably underlines that the key to any kind of successful third Grand Tour participation is always motivation.But as Kuss also said at the Vuelta a España team presentation in Monaco on Thursday evening, rather than set a GC goal as a priority from the word go, he's going to look at where he's standing overall at the end of what is a very mountainous first week, and take it from there."We'll see after the first week. For me, the main thing is to win a stage, but we'll get into the race, then see how it's going," Kuss told ."There are so many mountain stages, so many potential breakaway stages, that you never know what can happen. So in the first week, we'll take it one day at a time and see how it goes. The main things are the feelings, and I am feeling good and mentally motivated, and that is what is most important."Rather than ruling it out completely, then, Kuss simply gives the impression that he'll let the race decide for itself. As he put it to , "You never know."Certainly, he makes it clear that if it's a question of priorities, right now going for a top 10 position overall – in contrast to going for the highest places overall – has less appeal than going for a stage win."A stage would make this a great Vuelta. A position in the top 10 to me isn't so important," Kuss added in another interview with a small group of reporters. "But after the first half, we'll see how we're going as the team, what position we're at in the overall, and maybe look at other options depending on that."Kuss's attitude of not getting too far ahead of himself was exactly the type of strategy that brought such rich rewards in the 2023 Vuelta, of course, when he got into a break en route to Javalambre in the first week and then found himself very close to the top of GC after winning the stage.At the same time, given Visma-Lease a Bike have so many options for stage wins with riders like Wout van Aert and Matthew Brennan – to name but two of his best-known teammates – three years on, by not laying his cards on the table, Kuss is also allowing for lots of different scenarios to play out, both for himself and for his team."I'm feeling good. The truth is I always come to the Vuelta feeling motivated, and that's very important," he said. "You have to be on it mentally, because it's going to be a very hard Vuelta, right from the start. We have lots of options to look for stages, so we'll see how the riders are doing. We have a very well-balanced team."Stage hunting with Van Aert and BrennanSpeaking of his two standout teammates who will be looking for stage wins, the American said that Van Aert, recently a winner of the Tour of Denmark, "is in great form. It's going to be a big fight with Pedersen and Pogačar if he wants the points jersey.But he's particularly keen after what happened before in the Vuelta, too" – a reference to the 2024 race, when a previously all-conquering Van Aert crashed out and was badly injured whilst leading both the points and the mountains competitions.As for Brennan, taking part in his first Grand Tour, Kuss says that he's particularly impressed by the young British racer's ability to take almost everything that professional cycling has thrown at him in his stride, without losing his nerve."He's always super calm," Kuss told Cyclingnews. "It's different because he's such a good rider; that's not the same as a guy that doesn't know his capabilities starting a Grand Tour."It's different, too, for a sprinter, because it's such a hard race this year and he has to get through in the mountains. That'll be the main thing for him. But I can see that he's super calm and confident. He knows what he can do in these fast finishes. He's such a good rider."Most of the few sprinters present in the Vuelta estimate there will be just five or six sprints at most, compared to eight possible sprint stages in the Tour. But Kuss argues that the hillier terrain – which Brennan has already shown he can handle well before an actual bunch sprint, both in races like the Tour de Pologne and the Volta a Catalunya – will benefit the 21-year-old."The climbs take the edge off the sprint stage. If you have just the pan-flat stages where everybody's full of energy, then the sprints can be more chaotic," Kuss points out. "We don't have the lead-outs for that in our team, either, so I think that Vuelta-style sprints will be good for him."As for which stages will be good for Sepp Kuss, the American points to stage 4 in Andorra – where he won a mountainous trek in the Tour back in 2021 – as one possible target, given he's racing on home soil there and knows the roads extremely well. But further down the line there are plenty of other options, too, which could favour him even more."The stage to Andorra would be very nice, but I'm not sure if it's ideal, even if it's always nice to race there," he said. "But the ones that are in the third week with those very long climbs will be very good, and stage 9 in Alicante" – to the first-category Alto de Aitana, last tackled in 2016 – "is also good."By which point, too, Kuss will have a much better idea about a possible Vuelta GC bid and what his options are. But whatever happens in that regard, for a born climber like Kuss, any chances to shine in the mountains – and there are plenty of those in this year's Vuelta – are always too good to miss.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'A bit of a rollercoaster of a season' – Ally Wollaston sets her sights on Track Worlds after going 'back to the drawing board' at Tour of Britain Women
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: New Zealander Ally Wollaston has experienced the highs and lows of racing, with three early-season victories and a Grand Tour-winning team effort giving way to a recent battle for form.The 2025 Tour of Britain Women champion described her 2026 campaign as both a "mixed bag" and a "rollercoaster", and, as she heads towards the final months of a long year, she's aiming to get back on track, both literally and figuratively.Wollaston won't be taking a second Tour of Britain title this year, instead forming part of FDJ United-SUEZ's support team for Lauren Dickson on the queen stage at The Great Orme in Llandudno. Speaking after the finish, she said that she's hoping to refind her form and confidence ahead of big late-season goals."Personally, it's been a pretty mixed bag for me. I came into this week with a little bit of uncertainty, I'd say. I was a little bit ill last week, and just probably a lack of road racing for me," she told ."So just trying to find the legs and a bit of confidence in the peloton again, I'd say for this week, has been my goal."Obviously we came here with a really strong team with Lauren, and we're really proud of the job that she did today. It was a brutal, brutal climb, and she did really well, so we're super proud of her."Wollaston's mixed bag looks impressive from the outside, even if she isn't pleased with recent form. The 25-year-old enjoyed a flying start to the year, taking two stages and the points jersey at the Tour Down Under, plus a second career New Zealand road title and a second Cadel Evans Great Ocean Road Race win in as many years.In March, Wollaston took seventh in Milan-San Remo, and in May she helped Demi Vollering take home the maglia rosa at the Giro d'Italia Women. Off the bike, she graduated with her law degree, and more recently, she picked up team pursuit silver at the Commonwealth Games while narrowly missing out on adding bronze in the points race."I'd say a bit of a rollercoaster of a season for me. Nothing drastically gone wrong, just yeah, a little bit sub-par at the moment," Wollaston said."It's not to say it's been an unsuccessful season. But as athletes, you just want to be going good all the time, and unfortunately, that's not the way it's been going for me the last few months. I'm confident that after this solid week of racing, my form will come up."A host of other riders in the Tour of Britain Women peloton are using the race to build up for the Road World Championships in Montreal at the end of September. For Wollaston, however, it's all about the Track Worlds in Shanghai, running October 14-18, with the Los Angeles Olympic Games in 2028 her long-term target."I've still got some big goals and ambitions for the rest of the season with the Track Worlds coming up in October, so yeah, I'll just reset and focus on that for the next few months," said Wollaston, a World Champion in Elimination and Omnium two years ago."Just coming into the Olympics in L.A., I'm starting to get a little bit of tunnel vision, I'd say, for the track. So, I'm certainly leaning towards that."Wollaston's battle for form in recent months has made switching between road and track more challenging than usual, she said. But she's identified her weaknesses and is now focused on the future."For me, I find it really mentally refreshing to jump between the two. I think this season has been a little bit tricky trying to juggle them and trying to be the best at both, and timing that. I'd say I've definitely struggled with that this season."In previous seasons, I've maybe had it mapped out a little bit more than this season. I feel like I've just been floating through the season a little bit without some real targets. So, I think definitely back to the drawing board for me, and just try to structure out the next two years to L.A. maybe a little bit clearer."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'I gave everything I had, and cycling gave me everything in return' – Julian Alaphilippe confirms his career is over
item.content:encoded: Julian Alaphilippe confirmed his retirement from professional cycling with immediate effect, saying he is stopping "not with sadness, but with immense gratitude". The 34-year-old Frenchman, winner of two road race world titles and six Tour de France stages, had a contract with Tudor Pro Cycling for 2027 but has decided to bring an early end to his career. News of Alaphilippe's retirement was reported on Thursday evening, and confirmed by the rider himself on Friday evening. "It is with a very particular emotion that I write these few words to announce the end of my sporting career," Alaphilippe wrote in a social media post."After much reflection, I had the honour of closing this chapter of my life on the Champs-Elysées, by way of Montmartre in Paris, on the final stage of the Tour de France."I feel enormous gratitude for having been able to work with, meet, or simply cross paths with so many wonderful people throughout my career. And a great deal of luck, too, to have made some of my dreams come true, and to have lived through emotions that will stay with me forever."Pride at having contributed to so many successes for all my teams. And at having been able to let you live them too. You have always supported me so much, even in the hardest moments. "Before coming back to you to share what comes next, simply a big THANK YOU from the bottom of my heart.”Alaphilippe turned professional with the QuickStep team in 2014 and quickly announced himself as a star of the sport, with an explosive climbing style and a helping of panache that made him a darling of fans in France and beyond. His career catapulted to world-class status in a 2018 season in which he won 12 times, including La Flèche Wallonne and two stages of the Tour de France, plus the polka-dot jersey. And he went up a gear from there, finishing fifth overall at the 2019 Tour after an extraordinary 14-day stint in the yellow jersey, following Classics titles at Milan-San Remo and Strade Bianche. In the delayed 2020 season he won a fifth Tour stage and wore yellow again, before winning his first World Championship with a devastating solo attack in Imola. Despite a trickier 2021, he won another Tour stage in style, and went on to repeat his World Championship success with an electrifying victory in Leuven – arguably his crowing glory.That was the high point, and though Alaphilippe went on to win at the Dauphiné in 2023 and the Giro d'Italia in 2024, he had begun a decline that has now brought his career to an early end. His final victory was last year's GP de Québec, won with a typically daring late solo attack. "I’m a kid from Saint-Amand-Montrond who started out in cyclo-cross and playing the drums at musette dances with my father. If you had told that kid one day that he would wear the yellow jersey for fourteen days and become a two-time world champion, he would never have believed you. None of this was something I was owed. It was a gift. A gift from many people," Alaphilippe said in an interview on his Tudor team's website. Asked why he'd made this decision, he said: "Because it’s the right time. I’ve always raced on instinct, attacking when my legs were burning, not when the numbers told me to. I made this decision in the same way. I woke up one morning at a training camp and I felt it: this is my final year. Without sadness."I gave everything I had, and cycling gave me everything in return,” he added. "That’s why I can say it with a smile: I’m stopping. Not with sadness, but with immense gratitude. To all the fans who carried me up every climb: thank you. Thank you for everything."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'We're looking for the green jersey, but it'll be difficult' - Kaden Groves tips Tadej Pogačar as potential rival in hunt for Vuelta a España points classification
item.content:encoded: Everybody knows that Tadej Pogačar hopes to add the red jersey of race leader in the Vuelta a España to his collection of Grand Tour triumphs this summer, but might he be in the running for the green jersey of points leader as well?That's exactly what Australian sprinter Kaden Groves is thinking, himself a winner of the Vuelta's green jersey twice in the last three years, and back aiming for the top spot again in the 2026 race.The Alpecin-Premier Tech rider is gunning for at least one stage win in the five flat - or not so hilly at the least - days that feature on this year's Vuelta course, but the 27-year-old also has hopes of adding a third green jersey in Granada on September 13.However, as Groves told he believes the way the intermediate sprints have been placed in the stages means there's every chance that, intentionally or not, the top favourite for the overall could take green as well."One stage win for me would be great, but we're also looking at the green jersey, although it'll be difficult," Groves said."A lot of the intermediates are towards the ends of stages so it's something that Tadej [Pogačar] could be collecting along the way, too."Globally, Groves says, he figures there are five chances of sprints, "maybe one more or less depending on if the break isn't too strong." But if the first one isn't until late in the second week, stage 5 into Roquetes just inland from the Mediterranean coast, that could be a benefit in disguise.The Australian has had a very tough year, with injury seeing him out of the Tour of Italy, his first Grand Tour, on stage 4 following a very early crash. He's still hunting his first win since the Tour de France late last year, in fact, taken in a spectacular solo break at Pontarlier just 24 hours before the race ended in Paris."It's been an up-and-down year, but I wouldn't be here if I wasn't in some sort of level and stage 5 being maybe the first real sprint stage that should give me a chance to ride into it."The Vuelta is a race for which Groves still has a soft spot too, because it was where he took his first-ever Grand Tour win in Cabo de Gata, way back in 2022. Since then there have been six more victories in the Vuelta alone as well as two stage wins in the Giro and that Tour win - just to focus on the Grand Tours. But his victory of four years ago on a day of baking heat on the southern Spanish coastline remains a very special one."It all happened on the same day that we lost [then teammate] Simon Yates to COVID-19, too," Groves added, "so it was a nice way to finish a day which had started out very rough."Fast forward four years, and Groves is racing what may, according to strong rumours, be his last Grand Tour with Alpecin-Premier Tech. But if that's the case - and it's yeat to be confirmed - he feels he has a solid line-up of support riders and teammates to help him claim at least one last Grand Tour stage win, and for the team to go for their own options as well."The leadout's fine, I've got Sente [Sentjens] and Lindsay [De Vylder], it's their first Grand Tour so it's a good opportunity for both of them as well."Then around them there's a few experienced guys like Michael Gogl for the early part, then we have the second part of the team being climbing support like Hugo [Houle], Gal [Glivar], Francesco [Busatto] and again Michael. So I think we've got chances on all sides."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Treasury Whiplash, US Debt Hits $40T | Bloomberg Money 8/21/2026
item.content:encoded: Bloomberg Money takes the pulse of your financial life, powered by the reporting of our global newsroom. Today's guests: Rebecca Patterson, Council on Foreign Relations Senior Fellow, and Kevin Gordon, Charles Schwab Head of Macro Research & Strategy. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Khosla Ventures Bets on AI’s Next Frontier: Science
item.content:encoded: Khosla Ventures is backing Discovery Loop, a new AI startup founded by former Google leaders including Jeff Dean that aims to dramatically accelerate scientific experimentation. Khosla Ventures Managing Director Samir Kaul explains why the firm quickly decided to invest, and why he believes the opportunity could be as profound as frontier AI models. He also discusses why soaring technology valuations are forcing venture investors to rethink what “seed stage” even means. He joins Ed Ludlow on "Bloomberg Tech." (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Meta Safety Trial Could Reveal What Zuckerberg, Others Knew
item.content:encoded: Meta is facing a landmark legal battle with 29 states accusing the company of deliberately designing its platforms to keep children hooked while misleading the public about their safety. George Washington University law professor Mary Anne Franks explains the state and federal claims, why the case has drawn comparisons to tobacco litigation, and why the biggest consequence may not be the potential financial penalty, but what internal documents reveal about what Meta knew and when. She joins Ed Ludlow on "Bloomberg Tech." (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Wall Street Struggles to Absorb AI’s Debt Boom
item.content:encoded: Broadcom is lining up another massive bet on AI. Bloomberg has learned the chipmaker is in talks to raise more than $60 billion in debt to help Anthropic and others secure chips and computing power. The deal highlights a bigger concern hanging over the AI trade: the cost of funding it all. Erica Klauer, Science and Technology Partners founder and CIO, discusses concerns around circular financing and why the AI buildout is so challenging. She joins Ed Ludlow on "Bloomberg Tech." (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Anthropic Preps for Blockbuster Public Listing | Bloomberg Tech 8/21/2026
item.content:encoded: Bloomberg’s Ed Ludlow takes a look at Anthropic as the AI company expects to match or top the size of SpaceX's record-setting IPO. Plus, sources say Broadcom is in talks to raise more than $60 billion in debt to help Anthropic and others secure chips and computing power, and all eyes are on Nvidia as the chipmaker reports earnings next week. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Anthropic Aims to Match or Top SpaceX IPO
item.content:encoded: Anthropic is aiming for an IPO that could make history, expecting to match or even top SpaceX's record-setting debut, according to sources. The maker of Claude could file publicly by the end of this month. The company raised $65 billion in May at a $965 billion valuation. Bloomberg's Shirin Ghaffary, who leads coverage of Anthropic, and Bloomberg's Liana Baker, who leads the deals team, join Ed Ludlow on "Bloomberg Tech." (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Robinhood's Guild on AI, Markets & Risks
item.content:encoded: Robinhood's Stephanie Guild discusses the impact of major AI IPOs, market concentration risks, opportunities in healthcare and compute infrastructure, and why investors should balance AI exposure with cash flow-focused, defensive assets. (Source: Bloomberg)

item.title: Kortijk Koerse: Sofie van Rooijen out-sprints Charlotte Kool for a second career victory in Belgian race
item.content:encoded: Sofie Van Rooijen (UAE Development Team L'IMAD) out-sprinted Charlotte Kool (Fenix-Premier Tech) to win Konvert Kortijk Koerse. Kathrin Schweinberger (Human Powered Health) completed the podium from the bunch sprint.It was the second time in three years that Van Rooijen conquered the laps on the Flemish roads, last edging Chiara Consonni (UAE Development) and Daria Pikulik (Human Powered Health) in 2024. This time Rooijen had time to raise her arm to celebrate on the wet road from overcast skies and rain. It was her first victory in 10 months.The Friday race attracted six top level WorldTour teams, all present in Belgium for a series of three one-day races on the Flemish roads, of which this was the last. Kool took the win on Thursday at GP Lucien Van Impe.For Schweinberger, a third-place finish in the rain and across the cobbles was redemption for a DNF from the day before, where she crashed out.Now in a fifth edition, the UCI 1.1 race started and finished in Kortrijk and sent riders on a flat course of 127.6km with two large loops south of the city before finishing with six loops of 9km to close the day. Two ascents of the cobbled Beerbosstraat on the opening loops added an early challenge, but with only 842m of climbing the race seemed like one for the sprinters. A pair of riders formed the day’s breakaway, Loes Adegeest (Lidl-Trek) and Femke Markus (SD Worx-Protime) building a lead onto the closing circuits. But the flat terrain allowed the sprinters to reengage and on the final circuit the WorldTour teams positioned their riders for a bunch sprint. The race attracted six top level WorldTour teams, all present in Belgium for a series of three one-day races on the Flemish roads, of which this was the last. However, it was the Continental-level UAE development that stole the spotlight.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews.
