item.title: Last chance to shop the Le Col Summer Sale – Grab up to 60% off the remaining stock across the Men's and Women's ranges
item.author: paul.brett@futurenet.com (Paul Brett)
item.content:encoded: The Le Col Summer Sale is like summer itself, drawing to a close. The premium cycling clothing brand has up to 60% off across its site, including some of the best cycling jerseys, bib tights, cycling jackets, and more.Stock is fairly limited, but I built myself an outfit from the remaining available items, and I saved almost £400 on the six items I chose.This included an outstanding £132 off the Le Col Pro Bib Shorts, down to just £88, from the usual £220. With Northern Hemisphere winter on the way, another cracking deal is on the Le Col Pro Insulated Jacket, which has 40% off. However, there is very limited stock showing on that, so you'll have to be quick to grab yourself one.I've also enlisted the help of my cycling friend Nicola Watson to choose an outfit from the Le Col women's range, which arguably has even better savings. Emma chose five items and saved an impressive £300 on her selections.Below you'll find the details on Nicola's and my own outfits, and don't worry, there are plenty of socks; you can never have enough cycling socks, right?Some readers may be aware that Le Col entered a period of administration earlier this year. However, it is now trading as normal again.The Le Col says the Pro Jersey is its most versatile performance jersey. Taking design elements and technical insights directly from the world’s best riders, the Pro Jersey combines advanced fabrics and a precision fit, honed for riders chasing personal bests, dominating local circuits or ticking off a hard training session.It comes in four colour choices, but only the berry red and electric blue are discounted.The Le Col Pro Bib Shorts have been completely redefined for modern performance. Built for cyclists who measure progress in new best times, chase marginal gains and expect high performance every time they clip in. Designed to deliver aerodynamic efficiency, next-to-skin comfort, and the refined details that matter when you’re pushing your limits.They come in two colour choices, but only the black has the discount.Le Col designed the Pro Insulated Jacket for committed riders who aren't put off by cold conditions. It features Polartec Alpha Active Insulation for maximum warmth without the bulk. Le Col say it's a high-performance layer for high-tempo training and hard efforts on the colder days.The Pro Insulated Jacket comes in three colours, but only the light blue pictured has the discount.Le Col says the Pro Gilet is ultralight, packable and engineered using advanced Pertex Quantum Air technology for targeted protection. The Pro Gilet is ideal for shielding against headwinds, fast descents, and as an extra layer when the weather changes.It comes in two colour choices, with the navy version having the most sizes.The Le Col Tech Wool Socks are designed to deliver a high warmth-to-weight ratio, ensuring they keep you warm while remaining lightweight. Le Col claims enhanced durability is achieved through synthetic fibres and reinforced seams. Strategically placed cushioning provides comfort and support in all the right places.It comes in two colour choices and sizes S/M-L/XL, but only the navy is discounted.X Rudy Project Spinshield Air SunglassesLe Col partnered with the legendary performance sunglasses brand Rudy Project to create the Spinshield Air. Featuring a deep horizon lens for maximum visual clarity, the modern design is lightweight and versatile enough to be worn off the bike too.Available in three frame and lens combinations, all of which are equally appealing.Women's Sport Lightweight Jersey The Le Col Sport Lightweight Jersey is designed to keep you at the front of the group ride while still sitting comfortably at the café stop. It features a bold limited-edition geometric print that comes in three colour choices, with the purple version carrying the biggest reduction.Women's Arc Commuter Shorts Le Col says the Arc Commuter Shorts are designed to deliver versatile performance and unmatched comfort both on and off the bike. Crafted to be worn with and without bib shorts, they offer a casual aesthetic for commuting rides or off-road exploration.They come in two colour choices and the majority of sizes from XS-L.Le Col says they have designed the Arc Cargo Bib Shorts to perform across gravel, road, and single track rides. They combine durability with a luxurious feel. Crafted from soft, performance-driven fabric that moves with your body, these shorts offer exceptional support and flexibility for varied riding positions without sacrificing comfort.It comes in three colour choices and sizes XS-XL. The Green and Grey version has the biggest reduction.Long Tech Wool Cycling SocksThe Le Col Tech Wool Socks are designed to deliver a high warmth-to-weight ratio, ensuring they keep you warm while remaining lightweight. Le Col claims that enhanced durability is achieved through synthetic fibres and reinforced seams. Strategically placed cushioning provides comfort and support in all the right places.Colour choices are limited and selling fast.X Rudy Project Astral SunglassesAnother pair of sunglasses from Le Col that are in collaboration with Rudy Project. The Astral sunglasses unite high-performance optics with modern design, offering eyewear that performs at pace yet feels equally considered for life off the bike. Colour choices are limited and selling fast.The Le Col Summer Sale is live now, and there is plenty of kit to choose from, and there is free shipping for orders over £130.If you are a Le Col Member then there are exclusive member only reductions, including the LC_CC kit.The chosen deals are from the UK site, but Le Col US is also carrying discounts, and worth checking out if you're US-based. Below you'll also find Le Col deals from other retailers, which show the best prices in your territory.

item.title: Vuelta a España stage 1 time trial start times – When Jay Vine, Wout van Aert, Tadej Pogačar and others take turns on twisting 9.6km route in Monaco
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: This year's Vuelta a España will be shaped across Monaco, France and Andorra in the opening days and position the GC for the final two weeks of climbing and hot weather in southern Spain. There is instant intrigue for the first leader's red jersey, which will be decided in an individual time trial across 9.4km of twisting turns, tunnels and legendary landmarks in Monaco. This is the first of two ITTs in the three-week race, the second a 32km test on stage 18. This opener is expected to take around 10 minutes to complete, filled with an abundance of corners, and most of the elevation gain of 83 metres coming in the second half.Action starts on Saturday afternoon in front of the Monte Carlo Casino and culminates on Boulevard Albert 1er, and passes alongside Port Hercules and the Louis II Stadium to replicate much of the famous Formula 1 circuit held each year for the Monaco Grand Prix. The opening 2km head for a loop to the north on a pair of out-and-back sections, The intermediate time check comes at kilometre 5.6 in front of the grandstands and large yachts in Port Hercules. Then the second half of the route heads south to pass through the Rocher-Antoinie tunnel, a loop of Chapiteau de l'Espace Fontevielle, a pass through the Rocher-Palais tunnel and then the finish line. Absent will be 2025 overall champion Jonas Vingegaard, who is out from injury, so bib number one will be worn by the most recent Vuelta champion on the start line, Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe). Last year the Vuelta a España had just one individual time trial, which was not until the third week, won by world champion Filippo Ganna, but the Italian is also absent from this year's Grand Tour.The first rider of 184 will be Diego Uriarte (Kern Pharma), going down the start ramp at 19:20 local time. There is no adjustment for spacing between riders as all will take the course one-minute apart, concluding with Roglič, who takes off at 19:20.The ITT runner-up to Ganna last year, Jay Vine (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) is back and will take the course in the top 45. Another 23 riders later, his teammate Joao Almeida begins his ride, one where he looks to improve from third place last year. Among the favourites for the ITT this year are the three riders just ahead of Roglič, Wout van Aert (Visma-Lease a Bike) starting at 19:17, Ivan Romeo (Movistar) starting at 19:18 and then Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG).For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'I would love to get selection' – Lauren Dickson continues breakthrough season at Tour of Britain Women, aiming at a World Championships debut
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: With a strong showing atop The Great Orme on Friday's third stage of the Tour of Britain Women, British racer Lauren Dickson showed that a mid-season collarbone break hasn't slowed her down.The 26-year-old approaches the end of her first season racing at Women's WorldTour level, having joined FDJ United-SUEZ from Scottish team Handsling Alba over the winter. She immediately settled into life at the top level with a series of impressive outings.As the Tour of Britain Women hit the North Wales coast for its queen stage on Friday, Dickson was up there among the GC contenders, racing to sixth place, 26 seconds behind stage winner Kim Le Court-Pienaar.The result was a sign of her swift return to form after injury, sustained in a crash at the Tour de Suisse, ahead of a potential debut at the Road World Championships in Montreal next month.After the finish, she told that Worlds selection was a "huge goal", but noted that she doesn't yet know if she's made the Great Britain squad."I would love to get selection for Worlds. That would be a huge goal for me, and I think the course is something that would really suit me. But I mean, that's up to selection," Dickson said."I think we play it by ear, but training's been going well. I broke my collarbone in Switzerland, and actually doing a lot on the home trainer, which I think sometimes helps you. So, we'll see what happens."Other than that, there are some races in France, which are also special for us as a French team. So yeah, doing some good performances there would be nice."Regardless of Worlds selection, Dickson's rapid rise ensures that she will certainly go down as one of the year's outstanding breakthrough riders.She impressed in the spring with second at the Vuelta a Extremadura and third at her third-ever Women's WorldTour race, Itzulia Women. In May, she played a key role in supporting Demi Vollering to her Giro d'Italia Women victory while also racing to 11th overall herself.Dickson said that her first season with FDJ could barely have gone any better than it has – bar that unlucky collarbone break, of course."I think I always knew when I joined FDJ it was going to be a big step up. But if you're surrounded by the best people in the world – both the riders and the staff – I knew it was the best place to learn and develop," she said. "They promised me that they would support me, that it wouldn't be too much pressure coming into the team, and they were true to their word. So yeah, I think when I reflect on it, I don't think it could have gone much better, but it was something I always hoped I would be capable of."She hoped to add another strong final placing in Britain to her palmarès, and she also had the blue queen of the mountains jersey to defend after picking up 12 points on the road to The Great Orme in Llandudno."We thought, why not? For me, it's a home race, and it's special to take the Queen of the Mountains. I consider myself a climber, so to have the category is something I really like to fight for. The stage win was also a goal, but Kim was super strong, and I mean, we came away with one of the two, so it's been a good day," she said."I think we really like racing aggressively as a team, and we knew that a smaller bunch coming into the climb would be better for us because it means the race has been hard."We would also like to improve on the GC. If it comes down to bunch sprints, we have Ally, our sprinter, with us, and that's also a key goal. But yeah, definitely keeping hold of the jersey is also an aim."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: South African racer leaves Tour of Britain Women after returning out-of-competition positive test for synthetic peptide
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: South African racer S'annara Grove has been provisionally suspended after returning an adverse analytical finding for synthetic peptide Ipamorelin, the International Testing Agency (ITA) has announced.Grove was racing for British Continental team Smurfit Westrock at the Tour of Britain Women this week and was a non-starter on Friday's stage 3, with news of her positive test announced later in the day.The ITA stated that 32-year-old Grove returned the positive test out of competition on July 28 while attending the Commonwealth Games for track competitions, held at the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome in Glasgow. She competed for South Africa at the Games, taking 13th place in the scratch race and 16th in the points race."The ITA reports that a sample collected during an out-of-competition testing mission conducted by the Commonwealth Sport on 28 July 2026 from S’annara Grove, a rider from South Africa, has returned an AAF for ipamorelin. The test was carried out in the scope of the 2026 Commonwealth Games, which took place in Glasgow, Scotland, from 23 July to 2 August 2026," the ITA stated."Ipamorelin is prohibited under the 2026 WADA Prohibited List as S2. Peptide Hormones, Growth Factors, Related Substances and Mimetics. It is prohibited at all times (in- and out-of-competition) and is a non-specified substance. Ipamorelin is a synthetic peptide used to stimulate the body’s natural production of growth hormone."The rider has been informed of the case and, in accordance with the World Anti-Doping Code and Article 6.2.1 of the UCI Regulations for Results Management, a mandatory provisional suspension has been imposed on the rider. The rider has the right to challenge the provisional suspension and ask for its lifting."The substance Groves tested positive for, Ipamorelin, is a selective growth hormone-releasing synthetic peptide which stimulates the pituitary gland. It mimics the peptide hormone ghrelin to stimulate growth hormone release.Ipamorelin is currently a research peptide, the benefits of which haven't yet been demonstrated in controlled human studies. As such, it isn't approved for human consumption.Unlike other substances, which have been commonly found in positive tests throughout cycling history, Grove's appears to be the first Ipamorelin positive at the professional level.There has, however, been a history of Ipamorelin use in North American sports, with several baseball players (Andrew McKirahan, Nik Turley) and basketball players (Wilson Chandler, Jodie Meeks) receiving suspensions after testing positive.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'A shame I wasn't on Kim's wheel in the final corner' – Liane Lippert second behind unstoppable Le Court-Pienaar on Tour of Britain Women queen stage
item.content:encoded: Movistar were the most active team on stage 3 of the Tour of Britain Women from Mold to The Great Orme in Llandudno, doing a lot of work to reduce the peloton on the hilly route through North Wales.The Spanish team was rewarded with a second place from German racer Liane Lippert, who delivered one of her best results of the season on the steep slopes of the climb overlooking Llandudno by the Irish Sea coast.She praised her teammates, including the likes of Aude Biannic and Sara Martín, for setting her up for the run-in, but said that nothing could be done to follow stage winner and new GC leader Kim Le Court-Pienaar (AG Insurance-Soudal), who launched her winning move just as the ascent hit its toughest slopes, 2.6km from the line."I'm really proud of my teammates. We knew it was the best stage for me of all five, so we put in a big effort, and it was really worth it," Lippert told at the finish."The whole bunch came back in the final, which made it a bit more hectic, but they positioned me well. It's just a shame I wasn't on Kim's wheel in the final corner into the climb; that was my goal."But I did the best possible effort and tried to keep the gap as close as possible."Lippert ended the day 13 seconds down on Le Court-Pienaar, who is in such strong form that she took third on Thursday's flat sprint into Blackpool. As such, there was little that could be done to stop her here, though the hectic start of the climb did prove an obstacle. After the scenic run around Marine Drive, Le Court-Pienaar went through the hairpin turn at the bottom of the finishing climb in perfect position, while Lippert and those behind her were slightly held up."There was also almost a crash of Lorena Wiebes, which made me and everyone else slow down," Lippert said."It was a bit unlucky, but honestly, [Le Court-Pienaar] was super strong. She saw that we all had a gap, so of course she kept on going, and I couldn't close the gap to her."With two stages left to run in the race, Lippert is now 26 seconds behind Le Court-Pienaar in GC and nine seconds up on Wiebes in third.Second overall would be Lippert's best GC result since the 2022 Tour of Scandinavia, and she acknowledged that taking the green leader's jersey off the Mauritian champion will be a challenge."It's hard. For sure, she's going to try to defend the jersey, and there's no uphill finish anymore. We will do a meeting later, and we will try."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: New road and gravel tyres from Silca signal a change in strategy for the Italian company
item.content:encoded: Italian company Silca has added to its range of bike accessories with a range of gravel and road tyres, which it says balance all the performance protocols associated with rubber.Better known for its lines of cleaning fluids, pumps, bags, tools and, more recently, TPU inner tubes and sealant, its new Protocol line of tyres provides a wide range of rubber for riders, all of which are tubeless ready.The gravel range features three different models, and one road tyre, though all come in a variety of widths, the company aiming to shake up the bike tyre market."Instead of traditional manufacturing methods that simply scale up road into gravel tyres, SILCA took a fresh perspective by distilling XC mountain bike performance into high-efficiency gravel and road tyres engineered for modern air pressures and rim standards," their press release states."The result is a tyre collection that is proven to be faster and more durable than the competition, both in lab and field testing."With Silca’s range of tyre accessories among their range, it’s no surprise the tyres themselves are designed with their Ultimate Sealant, tubeless valves, rim tape and TPU tubes and even their pressure calculator in mind. It is, in fact, those other products which inspired the company to produce their own tyres."Each product answered part of the equation. Eventually, there was one component left. The tyre."The RCR designated road tyre is listed as 'All-road' and comes in 29, 34 and 38mm widths, is optimised for 25mm internal hookless rims and is "built to eliminate unnecessary weight". The 29mm weighs in at 290g, while the 38mm is a claimed 350g.The three gravel models each have different intended purposes. Silca claim the RCG-1 is "the fastest gravel tyre ever made," adding the "directional tread is built for hardpack, pavement transitions, and high-speed race conditions."RCG-3 fits a mixed terrain tyre with extra puncture protection, "directional tread balances rolling speed with grip when the surface turns loose."Finally, the RCG-4 features an aggressive tread, enough to shed mud on loose surfaces, Silca saying it’s the tyre for "rides that favour control over speed."All of the tyres come in 45, 50 and 55mm widths and the brand has also developed a 32" specific version of the RCG-3 specifically for 32" gravel wheel bikes, which seem to be gaining traction. All of the tyres retail for £99. A rider known for his detail-focused approach to gravel marginal gains is Dylan Johnson. Over the past few years, the American racer has become well known for his optimised bike, wheel and tyre choices. Until now, Johnson didn't have a tyre sponsor, but it seems he played a key part in the development of the new Silca gravel tyre range and has joined the brand as a sponsored rider. In an Instagram post (embedded below), he explained, "I made no promises to Silca. I told them if the tyres ride well and test well, then we can talk about a contract."Johnson has raced on tyres from both Continental and Schwalbe in the past, but we should only see him on Silca rubber from now on.We will aim to test the new Silca rubber for ourselves soon. item.title: Deutschland Tour: Alessio Magagnotti lands stunning sprint win ahead of Paul Magnier on stage 2
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: Alessio Magagnotti (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) blasted across the final 100 metres and sailed past favourite Paul Magnier (Soudal-QuickStep) to win stage 2 of the Deutschland Tour. Iúri Leitão (Caja Rural-Seguros RGA) followed in third place.The 19-year-old Italian stunned with his first pro career victory, delivering for his German team. Soudal-QuickStep tried to get Magnier in position, but their work was scattered. Behind with all the teams trying to sort good lines, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe's Danny Van Poppel and Jarrad Drizners positioned their young sprinter.Magagnotti went full throttle from about 12 riders back, getting in the slipstream of Leitão and then getting daylight on the outside in the final 50 metres. "For me, it's amazing because I don't believe it," Magagnotti, who usually rides with the development team, said to broadcasters at the finish."It's I think my fifth race in the WorldTour. Danny [Van Poppel] and Jarrad [Drizners] had to do the big work for me and thanks for the win."Louis Barré (Visma-Lease a Bike) retained the overall lead, now six seconds ahead of Isaac del Toro (UAE Team Emirates-XRG).After the longest day of the five-day stage race on Thursday, stage 2 came in 18km shorter at 197km on a day for the sprinters. From the start in Schwäbisch Hall the single classified climb was tackled 38.9km into proceedings leaving a few rollers the next 80km and then a speedway of roads for the final 73km.The customary flurry of attacks began quickly, and it was a trio of riders who got away in the opening minutes - mountains classification contender Ole Theiler (REMBE l Rad-Net), Ben Felix Jochum (Lotto Kern-Haus Outlet Montabaur), and Alvaro Sagrado (Storck-MRW Bau). From this group, both Sagrado and Jochum were the mild threats for the GC leader Louis Barré (Visma-Lease a Bike), at just over three minutes back each, but there was a long way to go.Theiler had eyes on the stiff climb of Juxkopf, only 1.1km in distance but at a solid gradient of 10-14%. Sagrado and Jochum went one-two at the summit but the one point scored by Theiler moved him into the KOM lead, now one point ahead of teammate Miguel Heidemann.The trio carried on past the mid-way point and rain began to fall as did the time gap, going from as much as 2:30 to 1:45. Leading a long line of riders in the peloton were Soudal-QuickStep and UAE Team Emirates-XRG, keeping both GC riders and sprinters in check.The trio took all the points at the intermediate sprint in Landshausen and Oberhausen, but the peloton was closing down the gap, under 30 seconds for the final 50km, and the rain still making conditions dismal, which took away the normal sunshine in the area meadows filled with vineyards and villages.With 31km left, the peloton made their catch, UAE Team Emirates-XRG increasing the pace. The race got a bit spicy at the Bonus time sprint on offer, with Del Toro accelerating around a corner in Belheim to get the better of the race leader Barré and grabbed three seconds. Nils Politt led out his teammate and in the process took two seconds himself. The action disrupted the peloton as the final 20km approached, but a separation of riders at the front closed quickly and the sun succeeded in breaking through the clouds. The bell rang with 13.3km to go on a pass through the finish line, the peloton still all together on narrow roads through the countryside. Unibet Rose Rockets moved en masse to the front as did Lidl-Trek for the final two kilometres.Magnier was third wheel as his team tried to formulate a train in the final kilometre, but other riders infiltrated near the front. While Soudal-QuickStep, Caja Rural-Seguros RGA, Lidl-Trek and Bahrain Victorious riders spread on one side of the road, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe delivered their young Italian, who sprang from the bunch on a wide open path on the right and score the surprise win.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Renewi Tour: Jenno Berckmoes pulls off a heist to snatch stage 3 and the leader's jersey on Tour of Flanders-inspired day
item.content:encoded: Jenno Berckmoes (Lotto-Intermarché) pulled off a stunning heist to win stage 3 of the Renewi Tour, turning a late breakaway into success mere metres ahead of the charging peloton.On a route inspired by the Tour of Flanders, the 25-year-old Belgian went clear of a fragmented peloton in the company of Alec Segaert (Bahrain Victorious) over the final ascent of the famous Muur van Geraardsbergen. Despite only holding a narrow gap on the reduced peloton for much of the 33-kilometre finishing circuit, the pair of them returned to Geraardsbergen with a slender lead and a shot, with the finish line positioned half-way up the climb – on the cobbles of De Vesten but before the iconic steep section of the Muur by the chapel. Berckmoes attacked Segaert with 500 metres to go and surged clear as his compatriot was swallowed up by the charging pack. His own teammate Arnaud De Lie opened the sprint behind, with race leader Jasper Philipsen (Alpecin-Deceuninck) coming around for second place three seconds down, just ahead of Olav Kooij (Decathlon CMA CGM) in third. Philipsen was forced to hand over the leader’s jersey to Berckmoes, who also claimed 18 seconds in time bonuses – 10 for his stage win and eight during the ‘Green Kilometre’ on the Bosberg, shortly after the winning move was made.Having started the day nine seconds down, Berckmoes now leads the race by six seconds over Philipsen, with Kooij another six seconds down. In a race that was always going to be decided by seconds, and where the Green Kilometre bonuses can have a big influence as they did today, it's wide open as we head into the final weekend.The third stage of the Renewi Tour was a 182km journey from Celles to Geraardsbergen, taking in several classic climbs of the Tour of Flanders, including the Paterberg, en route to the finishing circuit that featured not only the iconic Muur and Bosberg combination, but also the Onkerzeleberg and Denderoordberg climbs. There were four non-starters after a crash-ridden stage 2: Kasper Asgreen (EF Education-EasyPost), Simone Consonni (Lidl-Trek), Tobias Bayer (Alpecin-Premier Tech), and Taco van der Hoorn (Lotto-Intermarché). The stage opened with two short laps around Celles, where the first breakaway was brought back and, as they headed to the Flemish Ardennes, replaced by a new three-man move containing: Julius Johansen (UAE), Frederik Frison (Pinarello-Q36.5), and Michiel Lambrecht (Flanders-Baloise). After the spate of non-starers, there were more non-finishers, with stage 1 winner Jonathan Milan (Lidl-Trek) unable to continue after his heavy crash the previous day, while those to crash out here were Sam Welsford (Netcompany-Ineos), Filip Maciejuk (Movistar), Albert Torres (Movistar), and Haimar Etxeberria (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe). The breakaway took their lead out towards the four-minute mark as they ticked off seven climbs, including the Knokteberg, Paterberg, and Oude Kruisberg, en route to Geraardsbergen for two laps of a 33km finishing circuit. The circuit started and finished on De Vesten, half-way up the famous Muur van Geraardsbergen, and went on, after the steep section to the chapel, to tackle the Bosberg, then the Onkerzeleberg and Denderoordberg, with plenty of flat roads in between. The gap to the break was down to two minutes by the first passage of the finish line with 66km to go. There was no real action in the main peloton until the first climb of the Onkerzeleberg, where Lorenzo Milesi (Movistar), Martin Svrcek (Soudal-QuickStep), and Niklas Behrens (Visma-Lease a Bike) attacked from the bunch and bridged to the leaders to make it six out front. As the pace intensified there were more crashes, Biniam Girmay (NSN) going down before another huge pile-up a kilometre from the end of that first and penultimate lap. Magnus Sheffield (Netcompany-Ineos) and Vlad Van Mechelen (Bahrain Victorious) were forced out as a result.That crash effectively split the peloton as they headed onto the Muur and under the finish banner, with Berckmoes and Segaert up in a split of seven that hit the steep section of Kapelmuur and swallowed up the day's break. The two of them forced their way clear over the top and survived to the Bosberg, where they shared out the Green Kilometre bonuses.The 40 or so riders left in the peloton were close at hand but never well organised, with Philipsen closing gaps on his own at one point, and a number of accelerations but no cohesive chase. When Laurence Pithie (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) attacked with 18km to go there was a huge lull, which allowed the Kiwi rider to settle into a long solo pursuit, but he'd never join the two Belgians, who were combining faultlessly. There was a big surge in the bunch on the approach to the final climb, the Denderoordberg, which did for Pithie and brought the leading duo back to within 10 seconds. But despite an attack from Tomas Kopecky (Unibet-Rose-Rockets), there was a new lull, and the gap went out again. That gave fresh hope to the leading pair, especially as the final couple of kilometres towards Geraardsbergen were downhill. The peloton chased, and split once again on the technical entrance to the town off the descent, and it hung in the balance. But Berckmoes delivered an almighty burst of power as the road tilted uphill to surge clear of Segaert and as he maintained his power over the draggy cobbles it soon became clear he was on his way to victory. Segaert was swallowed up, and the fast finishers hit out behind, but Berckmoes held off to cap a fine victory that leaves this race perfectly poised.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: A County Got Rich From Data Centers. Some Question ‘At What Cost?’
item.author: Cecilia Kang and Caroline Gutman
item.content:encoded: Loudoun County, Va., hosts more than 250 data centers that bring in huge tax revenues. But some officials and residents worry the county has become too dependent on that cash.

item.title: Tour du Limousin: Ewen Costiou wins the overall for a second time as Noa Isadore wins his second stage of the week
item.content:encoded: Noa Isadore bookended the Tour du Limousin with his second stage win of the week on Friday, the Decathlon CMA CGM rider winning from a small group.Having taken a solo victory on Wednesday's second stage, Ewen Costiou (Groupama-FDJ United) won the overall title for the second consecutive year, finishing a few seconds behind the stage winner on the final day of four.Isadore infiltrated a small group which the Cofidis team led off the front of the bunch in the final kilometre, eventually out-sprinting Alex Aranburu (Cofidis) and Alexandre Delettre (TotalEnergies).Aranburu's second place meant he took second overall with Mattéo Vercher (TotalEnergies) in third. Both men finished 15 seconds behind Costiou, though the Spaniard took second on countback.Taking the riders on a 178.7km stage between Nantiat and Limoges, stage four set the peloton another hilly day, with three finishing laps each containing a short climb.The day’s breakaway was quick to get away, Victor Van de Putte (Lotto-Intermarché), Arnaud Tendon (Van Rysel-Roubaix), Victor Jean (Elite Fondations), Jaakko Hänninen (Nice Métropole-Côte d’Azur) and Jean-Louis Le Ny (Venice Club Rouen 76) building a lead over two minutes. That advantage began to decrease as the race entered its final 60km, Decathlon CMA CGM and Cofidis slowly bringing them to heel. With the deficit just over one minute as the race approached 30km to go, a mechanical gave race leader Ewen Costiou a scare, though the Groupama rider was soon on a spare bike and heading back to the bunch, two teammates to guide him.The breakaway was left to dangle off the front of the peloton for a long while, though they were finally brought back 16km, a series of attacks punctuating the final. Mathis le Berre (TotalEnergies) managed to get a gap on the final lap, but was never able to threaten Costiou’s GC lead, despite having started the day only 38 seconds down.Noa Isidore (Fra) Decathlon CMA CGM TeamAlex Aranburu (Spa) CofidisAlexandre Delettre (Fra) Team TotalEnergiesPierre Gautherat (Fra) Decathlon CMA CGM TeamMattéo Vercher (Fra) Team TotalEnergiesKay De Bruyckere (Bel) Pauwels Sauzen - Altez Industriebouw Cycling TeamAntoine L'Hote (Fra) Decathlon CMA CGM TeamMatthew Fox (Aus) Lotto-IntermarchéSergio Meris (Ita) Unibet Rose RocketsRémi Capron (Fra) Van Rysel-RoubaixMilan Menten (Bel) Lotto-IntermarchéMaxime Jarnet (Fra) Van Rysel-RoubaixEwen Costiou (Fra) Groupama-FDJ UnitedRayan Boulahoite (Fra) Team TotalEnergiesAxel Mariault (Fra) CIC Pro Cycling AcademyYohann Simon (Fra) St Michel-Preference Home-Auber 93Killian Verschuren (Fra) Unibet Rose RocketsValentin Darbellay (Swi) Elite Fondations Cycling TeamFinal general classificationEwen Costiou (Fra) Groupama-FDJ UnitedAlex Aranburu (Spa) CofidisMattéo Vercher (Fra) Team TotalEnergiesAlexandre Delettre (Fra) Team TotalEnergiesAxel Mariault (Fra) CIC Pro Cycling AcademyAntoine L'Hote (Fra) Decathlon CMA CGM TeamYohann Simon (Fra) St Michel-Preference Home-Auber 93Mathis Le Berre (Fra) Team TotalEnergiesThomas Champion (Fra) St Michel-Preference Home-Auber 93Pierre-Henry Basset (Fra) XDS Astana Development TeamFor unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Vingroup Among Vietnam Stocks to Debut on FTSE’s EM Index
item.author: Nguyen Kieu Giang

item.title: Tour of Britain Women: Kim Le Court-Pienaar soars to spectacular victory atop The Great Orme on stage 3
item.content:encoded: Kim Le Court-Pienaar (AG Insurance-Soudal) soared to a spectacular victory atop The Great Orme on stage 3 of the Tour of Britain Women, moving into the overall lead of the race in the process. The Mauritian Champion attacked from the bottom of the 2.5km finishing climb on The Great Orme and soloed to the finish.She crossed the line 14 seconds ahead of Liane Lippert (Movistar) and 20 seconds ahead of Caroline Andersson (Liv AlUla Jayco). Le Court-Pienaar also takes the overall lead of the race, taking the green leader's jersey from Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx-Protime), who placed 10th.On an attritional, hilly stage through North Wales, Movistar did most of the work, reducing the peloton to fewer than 30 riders when the race turned towards the coast, but more riders came back on the run-in to Llandudno.Canyon-SRAM and FDJ United-Suez set the pace on the penultimate climb on the road around the limestone peninsula, leaving around 20 riders at the foot of the finishing climb where Le Court-Pienaar went all-in to win."It was hard. I wasn’t expecting to come so fast into it; we almost had to brake around the corners. The plan was to go from the bottom, and I got a perfect lead-out from my teammate Letizia [Borghesi], so I’m very thankful she was here," said Le Court-Pienaar after her victory. "I think it was the plan to just go all-out from the bottom, and my teammate put me in the best position possible for it. Then I just had to do the best effort I could to the top."Today I rode for Gladys [Verhulst-Wild], my teammate, she crashed out from the race. It was really sad to have her out because we came to this race together to redeem ourselves. We crashed out together last year, and she’s my roommate, so I’m very sad she’s not here. Today was for her.Going into stage 4, Le Court-Pienaar leads the general classification by 26 seconds over Lippert and 35 seconds over Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx-Protime)."I think you have to never be too confident," she said about her chances of winning the race overall."Last year, I had the leader’s jersey on day one and crashed out on day two. We just have to keep our heads on our shoulders and just keep doing teamwork like we’ve done for the past few days, stay positive and keep fighting until the end."Reduced group on final climbThree riders did not start the stage: Lotte Kopecky (SD Worx-Protime) was ill, Karlijn Koops (O’Shea Red Chilli Bikes) had crashed in the final of stage 2, and S’annara Grove (Smurfit Westrock) had been provisionally suspended for a positive doping test during the Commonwealth Games.Starting in Mold, Flintshire, the 104.7km stage wound its was through the hills of North Wales, including two classified climbs on its way. Although there were several attempts to get away, no breakaway could get established as the GC favourites’ teams kept a high pace, with Movistar doing the lion’s share of work throughout the stage.Lauren Dickson (FDJ United-Suez) was first over the Moel Fodiar climb to move into the virtual lead of the QOM classification, and the continuous up and down saw many riders lose contact, whittling down the peloton over time.A crash just before the start of the climb to Nebo took down Ricarda Bauernfeind (Lidl-Trek) and Karlijn Swinkels (UAE Team L’IMAD), though both could get back to the peloton and compete in the final.On the Nebo climb, Katrine Aalerud (Uno-X Mobility), lone escapee on stage 2, attacked from the peloton that was now down to about 40 riders, but Movistar did not let the Norwegian get away. At the top, Dickson took maximum points again and takes the QOM jersey off Steffi Häberlin (SD Worx-Protime) who had to abandon the race.After the descent to Llanrwst, Aalerud again tried to get away and again wasn’t let go. 25.8km from the finish, Le Court-Pienaar won the intermediate sprint in Dolgarrog ahead of Mischa Bredewold (SD Worx-Protime) and Wiebes, netting three valuable bonus seconds in the process17km from the finish, a group of dropped riders came back to the peloton from behind, increasing the size of the bunch to almost 50 riders. The race then stayed together until the Marine Drive, the road around the The Great Orme headland where the penultimate climb began with 6.7km to go.Zoe Bäckstedt (Canyon-SRAM) did one last pull before handing over to her teammate Soraya Paladin, both in service of Cecilie Uttrup Ludwig. 6km from the finish, FDJ United-Suez also came to the front, setting a hard pace for Dickson, before Riejanne Markus (Lidl-Trek) led the race around the headland with 4km to go.A total of 26 riders were left in the front group going into the short descent to the foot of the finishing climb, and while Bauernfeind had brought Fleur Moors (Lidl-Trek) to the front, Borghesi was in third position with Le Court-Pienaar on her wheel.The Mauritian Champion took the inside line through the hairpin turn into the climb and accelerated right away, never looking back until the top. Behind her, a chase group of Lippert, Femke de Vries (Visma-Lease a Bike), Wiebes, and Moors formed from which Lippert then went solo, trying to limit her time loss and finishing runner-up at the top. Wiebes lost contact further up on the climb and finished in tenth place, 37 seconds down, while Caroline Andersson (Liv AlUla Jayco) came from behind to take third place.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Manchester United’s midfield rebuild leaves Carrick with no excuses
item.author: Jamie Jackson
item.content:encoded: Signings of Tielemans and Santos have addressed an area that has been problematic since the manager himself stopped playingEd Woodward to MUTV in July 2015: “When people see Bastian Schweinsteiger on the team sheet, that’s going to send some shivers down the spine.” This prediction by Manchester United’s then executive vice-president, about Louis van Gaal’s new midfield signing, proved to be badly off‑target as the World Cup-winner’s career at the club proved to be a disappointment.Two years after Woodward’s bullish statement, Schweinsteiger departed for Chicago Fire with a paltry 35 appearances and two goals for United on his CV, having been forced to train for a while with the youngsters by José Mourinho, Van Gaal’s successor. Here, in microcosm, is the story of virtually all midfield recruits by United for a generation. The hope at the club is that this trend changed this summer, with the arrivals of Youri Tielemans for £35m from Aston Villa and Andrey Santos for £48m plus £2m in add-ons from Chelsea, with the manager, Michael Carrick, also closing in on Brighton’s Carlos Baleba.Continue reading...

item.title: Lotte Kopecky pulls out of Tour of Britain Women
item.content:encoded: Lotte Kopecky (SD Worx-Protime) pulled out of the Tour of Britain Women on Friday morning, not reporting for the start of stage 3 due to illness. The former world champion had played a role in the pair of stage wins claimed by her teammate Lorena Wiebes on the opening two days, but felt unwell on the morning of stage 3.She withdraws just ahead of the main general classification stage where she'd been expected to contest the victory. "Unfortunately Lotte Kopecky was not feeling well this morning," read a statement from the SD Worx-Protime team. "In consultation with the medical staff it has been decided she will not start today in the 3rd stage of the Tour of Britain. We wish Lotte a speedy recovery."The illness was not specified. Kopecky finished in the main leading peloton on both the opening stages, won in dominant fashion by Wiebes, and played an active role in setting up the first one.Friday's stage is an important day for the GC, with a punchy finish at The Great Orme. Though steep, it's not all that long, and would seem to suit Kopecky's talents. Wiebes, the overall leader, is punchier than a pure sprinter and will look to see what she can do but Kopecky's withdrawal is a blow for the team. It's also a blow for the rider, who won Milan-San Remo in the spring but has had a quiet summer and now an early exit as she looks to build towards the World Championships in Canada next month. item.title: 'It only depends on my legs' – João Almeida eyes possible 'Plan B' GC bid alongside teammate Tadej Pogačar at Vuelta a España
item.content:encoded: UAE Team Emirates-XRG may not have only Tadej Pogačar aiming for the general classification in the Vuelta a España this August. The Slovenian's Portuguese teammate João Almeida says he's not ruling out acting as a 'Plan B' for the squad, although it hinges entirely on his feelings in the opening stages of this year's race."It only depends on my legs, I'll see how I go in the first few days, and then we'll see," Almeida told at the teams presentation in Monaco on Thursday evening.The 28-year-old had a difficult build-up to the Vuelta a España, with a crash-out at the Tour of Pologne curtailing his preparation in his final race before the Spanish Grand Tour. And that was only the latest chapter in what has been a difficult season for the Portuguese racer, who was beset by an illness in the spring and suffered through six stages of the Tour Auvergne-Rhône Alpes before taking another break from racing. On the other hand, Almeida was the rider who ran overall winner Jonas Vingegaard (Visma-Lease a Bike) the closest in last year's Vuelta a España, taking second overall and clinching a spectacular stage win on the Angliru. He also has a third place in the Giro d'Italia and a fourth place in the Tour de France in his palmares, but the 2025 Vuelta was where he took his best GC result to date."It's a race where I was successful before, but the past doesn't give us any guarantees," Almeida said."I have good memories from it, but in the end of the day it's all about the legs you have at the moment. Hopefully mine are not too bad."The first test for the GC contenders is Saturday's 9-kilometre, technical time trial through the streets of Monaco. But as Almeida sees it, the gaps that could be established there are minimal and the most important thing is to keep a perspective on the long term, rather than take too many risks. And being so short, the information that can be garnered by riders regarding their overall form is minimal, too."You learn a bit but not much to be honest, it's technical, so the risks you take can play into the result," Almeida said. "And I don't think it's worth it to take too many risks. Those nine kilometres - the time gaps are not going to decide anything at all."These days you have nothing to win and everything to lose. So it's just about doing some good efforts, control what you can control, cross the finish line safely and that's it."As far as the route is concerned, the Vuelta start in Monaco could hardly be further from Almeida's native Portugal. But having ridden four Vueltas to date, he's not overly troubled by the absence of stages near to his homeland, given how much he's raced in Spain. Rather, his main goal to see what he can achieve without any unexpected incidents or misfortune skewing his performance."I'm hoping for some nice days, just enjoying the bike and feeling good, and that's it," he concluded. "So long as there is no bad luck in the equation, the rest is completely fine."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Ogier set for WRC return after Rally Finland crash
'I haven't even enjoyed any training this year, it's been that bad' - Mikel Landa in survival mode at the Vuelta a España
item.content:encoded: It was 11 years ago and Mikel Landa rode what was defined at the time as the 'hardest stage ever of the Vuelta a España' through Andorra over more than 5,000 vertical metres - and ended up winning.This time round, when the Vuelta reaches Andorra on stage 4 and once again tackles a non-stop series of climbs, Landa's in a very different place."I'll be fighting to survive through the first week and then I'll see what I can do," Landa told reporters at the Place Grimaldi press centre. "This is the most uncertain Vuelta of my career, I've had a bad year, I'm on the bounceback from a very difficult injury and I'm certainly not at 100%."I'll try and ride my way into form, but it'll be hard."On the point of ending his time at Soudal-QuickStep, where he managed to finish fifth in the 2024 Tour de France and was viewed as a key mountain lieutenant for Remco Evenepoel, Landa's bad crash in the Itzulia, breaking his pelvis, left him out of the count for the Tour this summer.Instead, as he concludes the 16th season of his career at WorldTour level, Landa says he was determined to go to the Vuelta - "it would have been even worse if I hadn't" - but he is painfully realistic about his options."I'm just not in good shape, but there is no other option," Landa, part of a lineup which also includes mountain climber Valentin Paret-Peintre, told reporters."I'm racing without pressure, the team knows how I'm doing and so do I. I'll give it my best, it'd be worse not to race the Vuelta. Hopefully I can enjoy at least one day."I haven't even enjoyed any training this year, it's been that bad. But I have to be optimistic, above all coming as I do from such a bad situation."Landa has signed with his local ProTeam, Euskaltel-Euskadi - the squad with which he began life as a pro back in 2012, albeit in a very different structure - for the next two years. The squad wasn't chosen for the Vuelta or any Grand Tour this year, but he's not ruling out racing a three-week race again in the future."I hope that this won't be the last," Landa, twice third in the Giro d'Italia and twice fourth in the Tour de France, said. "I'd like to be back here again."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Julian Alaphilippe has reportedly called an early end to his professional racing career
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: Julian Alaphilippe may have already pinned on a number for the very last time. The rider, who is signed at Tudor Pro Cycling through to the end of 2027, is not intending to compete in any further races this season and will also forgo the final year of his contract so he can retire immediately, according to French news outlet. had also earlier reported that the 34-year-old was on the verge of terminating his contract, with following on with the news that its sources had confirmed that Alaphilippe's last race had indeed already been run.The French rider had certainly hinted at the Tour de France that retirement was on the cards, potentially sooner rather than later, despite the three-year contract he signed with Tudor running through to the end of next season.After battling his way up Alpe d'Huez, to finish 26 minutes down from stage winner Richard Carapaz (EF Education-EasyPost) in 29th, Alaphilippe said, with and a small huddle of French media gathered around him, that: “It’s maybe my last one, so I made the most of it, I gave everything, not with a lot of success but I didn’t leave anything out there." has contacted Tudor Pro Cycling for comment on the retirement reports and will provide updates when any official statement is made on Alaphilippe's future.Through his career the two-time road world champion won fans over not just with his success, but also his racing panache which delivered excitement regardless of whether it ended with a win or loss. In much of the decade he spent in the WorldTour with Quickstep the wins were regular and prestigious. Through that time – as well as delivering two back-to-back years in the rainbow jersey – Alaphilippe clocked up six Tour de France stage victories, spent 18 days in the yellow jersey, won La Flèche Wallonne three times plus added Milan-San Remo and Strade Bianche to his UCI win tally, which now sits at 45.The run of top tier victories, however, slowed heading into Alaphilippe's final years with Soudal-Quickstep and team manager Patrick Lefevere had become openly critical of the rider who had delivered so much success for the team over the years.Still, at the time it was seen as somewhat of a coup for Tudor to land the giant of French cycling particularly as they were eyeing a wildcard entry for the Tour de France, which they secured in 2025. It was hoped the move to Tudor at the beginning of last season would mark a turning point for the team and also for Alaphilippe, who was looking to get "back on the winning path".However, while there were some close calls in 2025 – with podium results at the Tour de France, Tour of Britain and Tre Valli Varesine – it wasn't until near the end of his first season with the squad that Alaphilippe scooped up his sole victory of the season, taken at the Grand Prix Cycliste de Québec. This year, even podiums have proven elusive. There have also been a number of DNF's for the 34-year-old, including one at La Flèche Wallonne, a race where he had managed to climb on the podium in five of his eight starts.In fact, four of his five races on the lead in to the Tour de France this year were cut short before the final finish line, though Alaphilippe did make it to the Paris finale at what now looks set to be his last Grand Tour and his very last race.

item.title: 'A huge step-up and a lot to learn' – Kate Courtney swiftly adapting to WorldTour racing with FDJ United-Suez at the Tour of Britain Women
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Kate Courtney's road cycling adventure continues at this week's Tour of Britain Women, where the American racer is getting her first taste of Women's WorldTour racing at the five-day event.She's already a multidisciplinary star, with two mountain bike world titles and several major gravel wins on her palmarès. Earlier this summer, she added the American road title to that list of triumphs before joining FDJ United-SUEZ in early July.Courtney soon got to work with the French squad, taking on a pair of French one-dayers, so how is she getting on and settling into her new surroundings?"It's a huge step-up and a lot to learn, but there's no better place to do it," Courtney told in Clitheroe ahead of stage 2 of the Tour of Britain Women."It was great! I think it was definitely a hectic day in the bunch," she said of the opener in Cockermouth, which saw FDJ place three riders in the front group."We had a lot of wind and some tight roads, so it's a really good place to learn and work on positioning."The worlds of off-road and road racing are very different in several ways, so making a switch from one to the other must take some adjusting. So far, Courtney has shown little sign of it being a tough one, however.Alongside her US road title, she finished top 15 at the French races, La Périgord Ladies and Le Picto en Nouvelle-Aquitane, and has finished among the top 30 in the opening days in Britain.Beyond the racing, there are new processes and people to get used to, with a Women's WorldTour setup such as FDJ a much larger team structure than those seen in mountain biking and gravel racing."I think in mountain biking, you have only like two or three riders as women in a team, and she was really the big leader in the last few years," team directeur sportif Lars Boom told at the stage 2 finish in Blackpool."Of course, I hope she will grow to be one as well in our team, but for sure she's not a beginner rider who starts riding in our team. She has a lot of knowledge about training, how she needs to prepare herself for stuff like that."So you really feel that she's a professional, and then it comes by learning and doing things in the race, and just getting the hours in on the bike, I think."Boom said that learning to ride in a large peloton is another challenge for multidisciplinarians like Courtney to meet. He said, however, that "she's doing well" in the "quite hectic" nature of the peloton in Britain as she races in support of reigning champion Ally Wollaston."Every day she's well-positioned and doing a good job," he said, while Courtney described her integration experience as a "unique" one."The team is amazing, and it's been really unique to get to start racing as a team and playing team tactics. I'm excited to see what we can do."So what can be expected of 30-year-old Courtney, already impressing in her first few outings on the road? Boom hinted at future expectations of big results, though now is the time for learning and adapting."For the moment we don't expect too much. Not 'not too much' – I mean we expect a lot, but we let her do her thing. She can make mistakes; she just needs to do what her instincts tell her to do in the race, and then it will be fine," Boom said."This will not be her last race of the team, but the last race before Worlds normally, so she will go back after this and do a good training block and prepare for Worlds. And then maybe she comes back to race some races in Europe."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'We can make quick decisions' - Megan Guarnier switches from driver's seat to race bike to guide US women's team at Philadelphia Cycling Classic
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: Three-time USPro road champion Megan Guarnier retired after 2018 but made a surprise return to racing earlier this year at USPro Road National Championships and finished 11th in the road race. She then continued director duties, staying stateside while Technical Director Tim Mitchell handled any international races for the CCB Kenetik p/b Levine Law Firm team. The two planned to co-manage the next big UCI race in the US, the Philadelphia Cycling Classic on August 30. Now Guarnier has found her way from a seat in a team car to the saddle of a team bike, headed back to a race she won in 2016, which was the last year for the "Philly Classic". The race is back and so is Guarnier."We have a few riders that will be racing Giro della Toscana Femminile with the US National Team and unfortunately, one of our riders, who was racing incredibly strong in Europe, had a season ending injury. We feel that it is important to show our support of the return of the Philly Cycling Classic with full representation from our CCB Kenetik p/b Levine Law Group team," Guarnier told .The four-day Giro della Toscana Femminile in Italy takes place August 27-30, and the roster was not confirmed yet for Team USA, but Guarnier had many fewer riders she could keep in the US for the Philadelphia contest.What does that mean really? It's not a stunt, she wanted a full squad. And she said it was a unique way to help her young riders navigate the 14.4-mile circuit."It will be exciting for me to be back in the peloton, allowing a first-hand account of the race in real time, as opposed to being in the driver's seat and hearing it over the radio."In this scenario, we can make quick decisions and execute confidently, while drawing on my experience from my time in the peloton. As I'm working with our riders on the road, we will also have one of the team directors, Tim Mitchell, in the car who has a great feel for racing dynamics."The US domestic elite squad brings USPro U23 silver medalist in the time trial and road race Jorja Bond and Ella Brenneman, who had top-10s in the same U23 races. There are also Lizzie Gunsalus, Sabrina Hayes and Elizabeth Grier, with the 41-year-old veteran Guarnier. It is a young squad, with the five teammates averaging half the age of their 'boss', most of them not even out of grade school when Guarnier took the victory in Philadelphia 10 years ago.Absent from the CCB lineup is USPro women's U23 criterium silver medalist Lyllie Sonneman, who broke her elbow and wrist while racing on a block of Belgian kermesees. She finished runner-up in two races and won GP Désire Goossens-Drongen."She was having such a good Euro block! She's super tough though," Guarnier said.At the pinnacle of her 10-year career in 2016, Guarnier won GC titles at the women's Giro d'Italia and Tour of California to secure the first-ever Women's WorldTour title, and in between she soared across 'Manayunk Wall' for the victory. That final year, the women's race and men's race both ended at the top of the tough 17% gradient in the Manayunk neighbourhood located eight miles away from downtown Philadelphia. This year's course will take in the famous Manayunk climb again, but on the original course used from 1985 to 2012 for the men and the first 19 years for the women's race, known as The Liberty Classic. The route will begin and end near Logan Circle and the Benjamin Franklin Parkway in downtown Philadelphia with multiple passes of the hilly circuit.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'Cars from the general public coming at me from all directions' – Maeve Plouffe narrowly avoids being hit by driver at Tour of Britain Women
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Less than a week after Finlay Tarling was struck and killed by a non-race driver at the Volta a Portugal, Australian racer Maeve Plouffe put rider safety in the spotlight once again at the Tour of Britain Women.19-year-old Tarling died during stage 8 in Portugal when he was hit by a driver who got on the race course after the peloton had passed through. Plouffe, meanwhile, found herself riding among non-race traffic at the rear of the race convoy during stage 1.She took to Instagram to detail her experience, which ended with a DNF, and thankfully nothing worse."A badly timed puncture ended up becoming a 30+ minute chase. I fought and fought really, really hard, but you can only do so much," Plouffe wrote, outlining her battle to stay in touch with the peloton before telling of how she was almost hit while doing so."On a side note, while the race convoy was still in sight and I was less than two minutes down, there were cars from the general public coming at me from all directions, including one that nearly hit me on a roundabout."Later on, the moto escort was wonderful and I felt much safer. But considering the recent devastating events in our cycling community, it's scary to see situations like this, when we know that this can have horrific consequences, especially so soon after suffering such a tragedy."Stay safe over the next stages."The Tour of Britain Women, like the Volta a Portugal and many other races on the international calendar outside of the very biggest, are run with rolling road closures. This means that police motos shut off junctions in batches rather than entire race routes being closed off, as is the case at races such as the Tour de France Femmes.Unlike that option, which is far more expensive for race organisers but greatly reduces the risk of such collisions, the system of rolling road closures can sometimes go horribly, even tragically, wrong. This week EF Education-EasyPost CEO Jonathan Vaughters said "I don't think [they] work that well" before noting that Tarling's death could've happened at many other races.Plouffe was the latest rider caught in a dangerous situation on Wednesday, and there's little doubt that similar situations will occur again, as they have several times over the years.Her team, O'Shea Red Chilli Bikes, told that they wouldn't comment any further on Plouffe's Instagram statement, but noted that they "take the safety of riders and staff extremely seriously at all times" and "continue dialogue with both British Cycling and the CPA regarding the safety of our sport."In a statement provided to on Thursday, British Cycling, which runs the Tour of Britain Women, stated that they are taking Plouffe's experience during stage 1 "extremely seriously", noting that they take rider safety "as a priority". Stage 2 of the race passed without any similar incident."We note Maeve Plouffe's comments about her experience during yesterday's race, and we're taking these extremely seriously," said Jonathan Day, Events Director of British Cycling Ventures."Rider safety is paramount and will always be treated as a priority in our planning and how we operate any race. We're reviewing what happened with Maeve and her team, O'Shea Red Chilli Bikes, with the seriousness and empathy these comments demand."We recognise this comes at an especially difficult time for the cycling community, so we want to reassure all riders, teams and fans of the sport at this time of how serious we are treating these comments."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'It could be an opportunity to be close in GC' - Opening time trial in Monaco enticing incentive for Wout van Aert's return to Vuelta a España
item.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
item.content:encoded: Two years ago, Wout van Aert (Visma-Lease a Bike) made his debut at the Vuelta a España, and needed only two days to earn the red leader's jersey. It was a short spell before he then relinquished the lead another two days later, though he came away with a haul of seven podiums, including a trio of stage victories.The first day of racing has visions of the maillot rojo dancing in Van Aert's head, but he said in a press conference Thursday it was just an opportunity and not a priority."Saturday was a focus I had in the last weeks, and we'll see how that unfolds," he said about stage 1 starting in Monaco with a 9.4-kilometre race against the clock."Well, I did a bit more training leading to this race. Because there's something to win, the time trial itself. But also it might be an opportunity to be still close in GC for the day after."Van Aert missed the Tour de France this year due to a training crash in June when he injured his elbow. Before that, he rode only a team time trial at Tour Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, which Visma won, and a TT early in the season at Tirreno-Adriatico. He returned to action at the Tour of Denmark three weeks ago, winning a trio of stages and the overall, though the five-day stage race did not have a time trial, so he had to deal with a delay in preparations for this ITT."It's been a long summer, a very different summer for me, and it's nice to come back to the Vuelta. I had to wait in the end pretty long to ride on a TT bike. But then after the Tour of Denmark, I could do the training how I wanted," he told the media assembled in Monaco, including ."I did the recon of the course yesterday morning. I tried to do it in traffic, had a little bit of a look. Honestly, I think it's a bit too technical. The last part they went, in my opinion, a bit over the limit of what you can do on a time trial bike. So it will be interesting to see how that goes."But in general, it's an amazing setting here in Monaco with all the buildings around and the coastline. So that will be for sure very special to race between them."The busy, twisting streets of Monaco hosted a time trial for the Tour de France back in 2009, and this version of the course is 6km shorter. Borrowing from the route used for the famous Formula 1 circuit, Van Aert knows there are many corners and punchy climbs."We go pretty quickly into the mountains, stage three, four, so we don't have a long time to take the jersey. But with the time trial and stage two, there should be quite good opportunities for me. I hope to be close, and it definitely would be a dream to wear it [leader's jersey] again," he said."I like this race, I'm really motivated, and yeah, I'm really happy we get close to the start now."I think it's clear we are here with more of a team for stages than for a clear GC goal, so that's obviously a bit different than usual. I'm a versatile rider, and on this course, I should have a lot of opportunities."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'I need to race smart' - Tadej Pogačar looking to complete the Grand Slam of Grand Tours in the Vuelta a España, while still looking ahead
item.content:encoded: "I don't know if it's even worth answering that question," was Tadej Pogačar's categorical reply when asked if he thought he could win the Vuelta a España without too much effort this August. "It's going to be a very tough race."Speaking just hours before the race, which saw him emerge as a Grand Tour star in 2019 when he finished third overall, claimed three stages and the white jersey, Pogačar's keenly anticipated return to the Vuelta a España will now see him fight for the only three-week stage race still missing from his palmares.Widely considered the greatest rider in the world, perhaps even of all time, the UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider has just racked up his fifth Tour de France win in seven editions and is considered the stand-out favourite in the Spanish Grand Tour. However, he was almost scathing when asked if he thought that the Vuelta would be an easy event to win in comparison."I don't know if it's even worth answering that question," he said. "Here there is a very stacked competition, why say much tougher in the Tour, because here you also have amazing talents on the startline. It's going to be a very tough race, it's going to be a hard one. Everybody that is here, I expect them to be in top shape and there are some very, very good riders here. It's never easy."Pogačar also pushed back at the idea that - as was almost possible in the Giro d'Italia in 2024 - he could lead the Vuelta from beginning to end. For one thing, he viewed the opening very short time trial as more one for the specialists, given its very technical format. For another, he wanted to wait until the first big mountain stages to have a chance to gauge his form, and for a third, with the Worlds, Europeans and Il Lombardia on the menu after the Vuelta, he did not want to, as he put it, "end the race destroyed.""I will have to see my shape in the first few stages and always thinking about the three big races afterwards," he said. "I shouldn't end this race completely destroyed. I need to race smart and then see in the first few stages how we approach it."That didn't take away from his overriding goal, which was to win all three Grand Tours, he confirmed, and that necessarily means he will do his utmost to finish the Vuelta wearing in Granada on the evening of September 13."It's been quite a short time after the Tour de France to come here, but I had enough time to recover, and this starts close to my home," Pogačar said. "So I'm looking forward to it, it is one missing goal from my career, so I will give my best to try and win."For me to win all three Grand Tours has been a big goal and dream for a few years now. So it's going to be important to be good here at the Vuelta."Pogačar recognised that the fact that the Vuelta was his first ever Grand Tour had often made him want to do it sooner in his career, but his team - never in favour of having their younger riders do two Grand Tours in a single year - did not encourage that until he was older."For sure I have nice memories of the Vuelta, I was a young kid back there, but now there's a completely different approach to any race. So it almost feels like my first Vuelta again."I would sit down in December [with the team] and see if there was the potential [chance to race], and everybody would push back the Vuelta before the Tour. But in my mind I wanted to come and start here in Monaco. I can't skip the Tour, but this year was the time."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'Just putting my socks on these last three weeks was the hardest' - Primož Roglič reveals scale of post-crash injuries and challenge to reach Vuelta a España startline
item.content:encoded: The Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe rider had a major training crash when he was hit by a car in July. The pain from the major hematoma he suffered on his right leg as a result was so bad, he said, that as recently as "10, 14 days ago, I couldn't do anything. Just putting my socks on these last three weeks was the hardest."Things have turned around relatively quickly, though, in the last few days, and Roglič said he could, finally, contemplate racing the Vuelta. But given how much of a hit his training has taken, his condition remains an incognito, and his ability to mount a GC challenge will be very complicated to calculate before the race hits the hardest stages.Roglič pulled a face when it was pointed out to him that three times in the past, in 2021, 2022 and 2024, he's managed to return to a Vuelta GC challenge after a bad summer crash and win. This time round, he said, things were so bad "it's been hard to maintain the positivity.""When the car hit then, at first I thought it was not such a big thing, the speed was super-slow, and I fell on my side and on my ass. Luckily," he joked - "my big ass saved me."But then there was a super big hematoma; I couldn't do much for at least three weeks. If you asked me 10 days back, I wouldn't say I couldn't sit on a TT bike."Just putting socks on my feet was the hardest thing for these three weeks. Luckily, at the end I could start to move. I still cannot lie on my right side, but I feel good enough to ride my bike and come here to start the Vuelta."The idea of a full training program has clearly been out of the question, though, with Roglič summing it up succinctly that "instead of preparation, I did rehabilitation. It's a bit different, I didn't plan for these things, but that's why I come here, I managed to do some training."After crashing, I couldn't think about sitting, nor even riding a bike."As for what that means, maybe stage 1 and a 9 km time trial should be fine. But then for later on, we'll see how it goes."Roglič also recognised that being nearly 37 and running out of chances was a motivation to come to the Vuelta, plus, for the first time since 2019, he has not done any other Grand Tour this year. Although he recognised, too, that there had been conversations with Lotto-Intermarché about a possible contract for next year and a move on from Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, it seems logical that that present, concern remained very much uppermost in his mind, too."I always say, the older you get, you don't get so many opportunities, particularly ones as big as the Vuelta, specially starting this year in Monaco, that's something special, too.. I didn't do any Grand Tours, yet this year, so it would be nice to race a bit longer."Rather than focus on Pogačar and what his participation meant for the Vuelta, he said, given the circumstances, he was just looking at his own chances of success or failure. However, while he played down the idea of a repeat of the Vuelta bounceback of previous years, he simply said he had to accept that whatever he could do would be as good as it got."I would love it, but for 10 days, 14 days, I couldn't do anything; I was still at exactly the same point as after the crash. It's hard when that happens to maintain the positivity.""But at the end you need to let it go, what will happen will happen. Either I'm in good shape, or I'm not. I just want to sit without too much pain and move without too much pain."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Jonathan Milan ordered to pull over as race leader is lapped by peloton following huge crash at Renewi Tour
item.content:encoded: Race leader Jonathan Milan (Lidl-Trek) rolled home on stage 2 of the Renewi Tour after a crash and a 65km struggle that saw him trail by several minutes and even have to stand aside in the finale as he was lapped by the peloton. The Italian, swapping his national champion's jersey for the light blue race leader's jersey following his victory on the opening day, hit the deck heavily in a huge crash on the finishing circuit in Ardooie. The race had been splitting in the crosswinds and tensions were high when an Alpecin-Premier Tech rider overlapped a wheel and jutted to the left, sparking a chain reaction that sent riders bouncing off each other and many to the ground. It was a sprawling crash that involved a good central chunk of the peloton. Jayco-AlUla's Amaury Capiot was seemingly the worst affected, his teammate Luke Durbridge calling for medical attention as he hovered over him, with Capiot soon taken away in an ambulance. Milan was also in a bad way and didn't get up for a few minutes. As he lay stricken initially, it looked as though his race was over. He had landed awkwardly and was clutching his right arm, with a grimace on his face. However, Milan eventually remounted and carried on. The peloton was already several minutes up ahead by the time he'd got going again, and there was no chance of getting back in. In fact, Milan could barely hold the wheel of his teammate Simone Consonni, who'd been ordered to wait for him, and at that point it looked unlikely that Milan would be able to ride like this for the 60km required to make it to the finish. But ride on he did, sticking with Consonni well behind the peloton as the laps of the Ardooie circuit ticked down, and the time gap ticked up, well into the double digits. There was, however, a spanner in the works on the final lap. He was so far behind that the peloton was actually coming up behind him, and the organisers, after discussions with the Lidl-Trek team car, ordered Milan and Consonni to stop and pull over. The pair of them stood and chatted at the side of the road before the peloton went past, and they could get going again, still needing to cross the finish line and then ride a whole other lap.They completed the race within the time limit and will be able to continue in the race on Friday on stage 3.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews.
